div.head: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
"SHE threw herself at his head, but she didn't get him at that." "Certainly not. Girls can't throw."
TEDDIE: "What are women's rights, pa ? " Pa: "Everything they want, my boy; always remem- ber that."

DE CAVERLY "How do Pen Dennis's poems seem to go? " Van Smith: "Oh, they go all right. It's their coming back that annoys him." FRIEND: "Do you know that I am at last be- ginning to understand your poetry?" Great Magazine Poet: " Heavens ! Is it, then, true that I am losing my cunning ?" "I HEAR your last tour was not much of a suc- cess ? " " No,t' sadly replied Mr. Barnes Tormer, the eminent tragedian, "the weather was so hot that it was a regular frost." ARTIST: "Do you wish your portrait in oil, madam ?" Patron: "I don't know. Oil is so un- settled in price." THE latest market report—sky-rockets have gone up. LAWYER QUIBBLE: "What was the greatest trial you ever presided ove-, judge ? " Judge Kidby : "Bringing up ten daughters, sir !"

_ "DON'T sit on this bench with me, George, please!" said Maud. "Why not?" asked George. "Because it is only strong enough for one," said Maud. "Then I say, Maud, can't we be made one?" suggested George. NOTHING TO RUB IT WlTlL—Little Clarence: "I heard pa talking last night about a baby being born without any hands." Little Bob; "Well, that's too bad! What will he do when he has the stomachache?" SOME SURE TO FIT lint.—" Now, here is some- thing that will cure you !" said the quack." "But nothing ails me." "Well, just look over the list of dangerous symptoms, and I think you will find that you are troubled in some way." IN YANKEE LAND.—" Feller citizens, I tells ye the English ain't got any business on these here shores, ner never had. We ain't got no use for their manners; we ain't got no use for their cus- toms ; we ain't even got no use for their language, when ye comes to think on it." "You are right," said a man in the crowd, "You get along without it first-rate."

A WARNING. - The conversation turned upon the fatal number, Friday, salt-spilling, and other superstitions. "It is not well to make too much fun of such matters," oaravely remarked Briclian- teau. "For instance, I had an old uncle who, at the age of 77, committed the imprudence of making one of a dinner party of thirteen." "And he died the next day?" Le Ribi inquired. "No ; but exactly thirteen years afterwards." A shudder ran through the audience. "YOUR family," sighed the noble saitor, regret- fully, "has no antiquity. Good-bye." She sat in a trance of horror. "Antiquity," she shrieked, when he had left her for ever. "Antiquity, for- sooth ! " When they found her she was calmer, but still bitterly cursing the impulse which had bidden her claim to be but twenty-three when she was thirty-seven. A Bfia Fisn.—" Speaking of fishing," said a brave and truthful son of the sea, recently, "they don't get any such fish nowadays as we used to catch. I remember one day some years aao we were fishing off Wooden Ball, when we hooked a halibut, and I can tell you he was what we called a ' hister.' We couldn't get him into the boat, but with the aid of flood tide, we towed him in towards Carver's harbour, and, sir, when we got to the mouth of the harbour we had to turn him up edgeways to get him in."

WOULDN'T FADE.—" Been buying a horse for my daughter to ride," said the ft man to the man with the spectacles. "Eh ? " said the spectacled man. "Yes. I picked out a nice bay, well broken in—tried him myself—and brought him around for her approval. She looked him over with as critical an air as I ever saw, but I'll bet cigars for the two of us you can never guess what she asked me after she had finished." "No, I can't guess. What was it?" "She wanted to know if I was sure the beast would never fade." FATHER (to the anxious one) : "Do you think you can live in peace with my daughter ? " Suitor: "I am sure I can." Father : "That is more than we, her parents, were ever able to do. Take her, my son; you are more than welcome." A PRoFEssioNAL SECRET.—An accomplished master of the art of stealing had to answer a charge of robbery in a Vienna court of justice. The prisoner at once admitted his guilt, but to the great surprise of the bench maintained a stubborn silence after one of the questions addressed to him. The presiding magistrate repeated the question: Tell me, how did you manage to abstract the watches, which were nearly all fitted with safety rings ?" The prisoner still hesitated to reply. At length he said, deeply blushing and with a timid voice :.." Excuse me, your worship, that is my
secret."

A FAILURE.—" Bridget, I want a pound of steak, a bar of salt, two ounces of pepper, a loaf of bread, and a pound of butter. Do you think you can remember them all, or shall I write them down ?" " Sure, ma'am, I kin remimber one by the other. When I hev bread, I know I want butter, and when I have steak I want pepper and salt." "All right, Go, and don't be long." Bridget was not long. She was back in a very short time, but with any empty basket. "Why, where is the dinner, Bridget?" "I couldn't remimber wan of them, ma'am." "Why I thought you could remember each article by the one before it." "Faith, ma'am, I had nothin' to rcmimber the furst one by."

I will now proceed with the wonder- ful performance of the magic egg-bag," &c, ADVANCE NOTICE.—We are contemplating pub- lishing a volume containing one million six hundred and fiftynine thousand nine hundred and one sure ways to exterminate flies. While we have not per- sonally tested the efficiency of every one of these recipes, we have been solemnly and gratuitously assured by persons of respectability that each is the only one which positively never fails. The book will be of such a size that, should none of the recipes give satisfaction, it can be used to smash the pests individually, with no further exertion than lifting it over tiem and dropping it. HE WATCHED HlM.—The interest shown in the droll doings and amusing observations of little Folks is proved by the success of recent works on the Eubject. Most of us have, some time or another, heard children come out with as comical things as any, invented or otherwise, that we see chronicled. Not long since a correspondent sent a provincial paper an anecdote of the kind referred to, of which his six-year-old boy was the hero. He says "I keep a shop, and sell fancy goods. A gentleman came in to buy something. It was early, and my little boy and I were alone in the house at the time. The gentleman gave me a sovereign, and I had to go up-stairs to my cash- -box. Before doing so I went into the little room next to the shop and said to the boy: "'Watch the gentleman that he don't steal anything,' and I put him on the counter. t‘ As soon as I returned he sang out: "'Pa, he didn't 'steal anything—l watched him.' "You can imagine the position I was in."
MR._ HARDACRE (just returned from city) "Tell

yet- what, Becky, I've been a darned 100 l to let my money lay in th' savings bank at three per cent. all these years, when they pay 50 per cent. down ter New York." Mrs. Hardacre : "I don't believe they pay no such interest." Mr. Hardacre :

"Oh, yer don't, Mrs. Smarty, don't yer? Well, I just loaned one hundred dollars at that rate ter day. I'll tell you how I done it. I met a right filick-look in' young man in front of the Astor House, and he says ter me, says he, Sir, I would like to borrow one hundred dollars, for which I will pay fifty per cent. interest." But,' says I, I don't know yer, and how am I to tell that you will pay inc the interest?' you doubt me, sir,' says he, I will pap you the fifty per cent. in advance.' Well, that looked safe enough, sul give him two fiity-dollar notes, and he paid one of them back for the interest right on the spot. I'm to meet him at the Astor House every year and get the interest. I tell you what. Becky—it makes me mad.to think what I've lost all these years."

1,70 w that we are nearing the holiday seaevu of the year, most people have begun to examine their wardrobes with a view to making any necessary additions before starting for the country or seaside, or whatever other place they may select in which to spend their holi- days. If it is to the seaside we intend to wend our way, then a bathing dress is an absolute necessity, for to stay by the sea and not bathe is not to be contemplated for a moment, and, naturally, for this purpose a suitable "dress must be provided. At most seaside places I know that bathing costumes of all sorts and sizes are let out on hire, but I cannot say that the idea of wearing a garment that has been worn by dozens of people before, in any way appeals to me, and I fancy that most ladies will agree that it is far pleasanter to possess a bathing suit of one's own. This need not be elaborate by any

means; in fact a fussily-made bathing dress neither looks well nor feels comfortable, and after all comfort while bathing is the main point to be considered. It is, however, quite possible, by following the design given above, to combine both beauty and comfort, and no reasonable woman can ask for more than this. The sketch here shown is meant to be carried out in flannel, but a thin serge could be used with equally good results. It is made in a combination fashion, having a short and fairly full tunic reaching almost to the knees, and displaying below it the full knickerbockers. This tunic is gathered into a band at the waist, and is ornamented round the bottom, a few inches above the hem, with a row of coarse lace, the same trimming also being used to finish the square-cut neck both back and front. The sleeves are composed of a short, full puff, neatly gathered into a band, and the shoulders are ornamented by square revers edged with a frill of the same material as that of which the suit is made. Dark-blue flannel would look exceedingly neat, and, if liked, the frills on the revers might be omitted, and their place taken by an edging of lace similar to that used on the tunic. _ _

I strougly advise any liidy who contemplates visiting the sea this summer, and who has not already a bathing costume, to send for this pattern, and at once set to work on it. Most of us, I suppose, already count a coat and skirt amongst our possessions; but, even- if this be so, a new design for so useful a g,atment is always acceptable. It cannot be said that the newest designs are always the

;The coat is so arranged that it can be worn either with fronts or blouses. It is cut open in the front and turned back with short, square revers which reach only to the bust. The belt rrangement is decidedly novel; a hole is made cu either side of the front through Which the v4iistband is passed; it goes outside the. coat at the back, thus keeping it well in place. The basque iS short and and the sleeves are finished with gauntlet cuffs. • The skirt is plain, and hangs in graceful tintes. • For making this costume, flannel, mohair,. or any similar material, would be suitable. and might be used with very happy effect. - If fronts are worn they can, of course, be varied according to the occasion. A very 1 retty one may be made quite easily by gather- ing a piece of silk into the collar-band, which should be plainly covered with silk.. Then fold apiece of insertion lace round the collar, cross the ends at the back, bring them round to the liont, and tie them in a bow. This willform a front like that shown in the sketch. • • • Gooseberries are just beginning 'ld be plenti- ful enough to us to be able to use them with- out any qualms on the score of undue extra- vagance. Gooseberry tart, fool, etc., are, Of course, Well-known, but doubtless many of. my ; ender; have not heard of gooseberry cake, and will welcome this new and delicious way cf serving the fruit. Stew about two pounds of the gooseberries with half a pound of crushed loaf sugar. Slice up four penny sponge cakes, and line a pudding-basin with thew, maging them fit in as well as possible. Now, put a layer of the fruit over, and arrange t he remainder of the cake in layers with the gi)o,-;eberries, cover with. a. saucer and small m!oi.-;ht, and place in the larder till the next dilv, then turn it on to the dish for servin- ocat the whites of two eo'crs on a plate to a firm „. li•oth, mix with two tablspoonsful ofonster i;Ugar, spread thickly all over the pudding, and sprinkle again with sugar. Bake in a cool oven long enough to set the meringue.

div.p: "WOMEN'S -CHAT.'

Although the official celebration v.,hich .attends the Queen's birthday is beyond her Majesty's control, she limits the hoine ceremonial as much as possible. The cake and other dainties she aßrccs to for the sake of the childrco,but it has long been understood that she will accept no gifts from any hut her immediate family. If her Majesty's birthday falls at Balmoral she retires to the Prince Consort's rooms, which have been pres.erved in the state in whith he left them, and spends the day there amid the s%d memories which they evoke.

div.head: UR ITIIBBHST THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY MAY 30. 1896 THE HIDDEN HAND;
div.p: UR ITIIBBHST THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY MAY 30. 1896 THE HIDDEN HAND;

Many of my readers who are not already acquainted with the fact may be interested to know that the Queen's birthday cake which was baked in the Royal kitchens at Windoor arid despatched to Balmoral,is m tde after a famous recipe brought from Germany and pre- sented to George IV. by the Duke of Cumberland, sou of George 111., and uncle of the Queen. Whipped cream and candied cherries form prominent items in the list of materi,, Is. The Royal grandchildren are very fond of these cakes.

It is said that the Queen is much displeased at the way in which certain inpmbers of the Royal family have indulged in festivity while still in mourning for Prince Henry of Battenberg. It is to prove her own consistency in this respect that the marriage of Princess Maud is to be a comparatively quiet affair instead of the more bril- liant display which both the Prince and Princess of Wales would have preferred. It is also for the same reason that the Queen has not presided at any of the Drawing Rooms this season. By the way the Princess Henry of Battenberg has followed the example of Her Majesty in wearing weeds of the heaviest description, anu these are especially noticeable in an age which usually reduces them to the slighest and most becom- ing limits. _ _

The late Mr. Benjamin Terry, father of Miss Ellen Terry, the well-known actress, who has recently died, was not at any time during his life connected with the stage. He was in fact for many years a tax collector at North Kensington, London. Although Mr. Terry had reached the age of seventy-seven, he was until quite lately, a familiar figure at first performances, in which any of his large and distinguished family took part. Speaking of the stage,few actors are as quick dressers as Sir Henry Irving, who is usually in the street fifteen minutes after the fall of the curtain. An hour is no un- usual time for an actor to take before be emerges from the door, as usually he has greese-paint to remove from his face, false beards to get off, his costume to change, and a modern toilette to make afterwards. Miss Marie Corelli can boast of quite a cosmopolitan reputation ; indeed in the number and variety of langu- ages into which her works have been translated she rivals M. Emile Zola himself. Versions of her novels have already appeared in no less than eight languages, and now it appears that the fame of the author of "The Sorrows of Sean " is more noised abroad than ever, for " Barabbas" and " A Romance of Two Worles" have lately both been rendered in Hindustani. The popularity of swimming as a recreation for our sex is making tremendous strides year by year. There is no doubt that this healthful exercise ought to be re- garded as part of every girl's education, and it is in- teresting to learn that in this particular direction the Queen has, yet again, set an example all mothers would do well to emulate. Her Majesty's daughters learned to swim at quite an early age, and the Princess of Wales, her daughters, and the Duchess of York are all very fond of the water. .The Empress of Austria is a most clever swimmer and has been known to perform some remark- able natatory tricks, and indeed all the Princesses ot the. Austrian reigning family are good swimmers. The Ger- man Empress and the sister of the Emperor are also fine swimmers and so is the Queen Regent of Spain, who ex- cels in all manner of feats in the water.

The black waist sash is engaging considerable favour in Paris where indeed no gown seems to be complete ' without it, and certainly it is of infinite more grace than the scaly sequin and white leather belts, which are still struggling tor existence over here. Wide belts of black satin, secured on the left side with large pearl buttons are quite a novelty at the present moment, and are decidedly becoming to all save those Vs; whom nature has been economical in the matter of waist length. Irish crochet is to have a real innings this season. It has during the past year or so made several unsuccess- ful bids for favour, but now the sun of fashion seems likely to fairly beam upon it. It is without doubt a good trimming, having a much richer effect than lace,and be- ing .nore suitable for collars and belts than embroidery, which is not consistent with simple gowns. Rose pink batiste is the very latest idea for women's underwear, and pink corsets to match are considered in- dispensable. There is very little doubt, however, that before long we shall once more return to the fine white longcloth we all in our hearts prefer above every other fabric for underwear. Printed and spotted muslins abound on every side,and many of the gowns preeared for Ascot this year, built of this material, are positive dreams of I evilness. By the way, there will be no Royal party at Bagshot Park for Ascot this year,but the Prince:of Wales,the Duke of York, and the Duke of Tech, according to present arrange- merits, will stay at Cumberland Lodge for the race week. Flowers in London town seem lovlier and lovlier each season, and more and more money seems to be spent on them. At a reception and dance I attended last week,a Louis XVI. design was used for the staircase which was done with wreaths of orchids, azalias and roses, all in tones ot gold, and tied up with pale gold-hued Louis XVI. bows, in the centre of which there was a little gold shaded electric lamp. The effect was that of fairyland. Then in the flower figure of :he Cotillon, sunshades profusel3, decorated with roses were distri- buted to all the women as well as clusters of roses for , their gowns, and all the men had buttonholes of the , same flowers. The effect was simply lovely and the per- fume delicious. I notice this year that women are wear- ing natural flowers much more than they did. Person- ally I mush prefer this mode, although it has its draw- back. Natural flowers so soon fade, especially in a heated ball-room, and one hates to See them dying. It appears that at last an Australian has started up with sufficient-temerity to attack the rabbit question, which is the cause of so much deep thought in that country. The scheme is to communicate to the rabbits the hereditary disease which some years ago carried off all the cats in Queensland. But, one cannot help think- ing that if all tbe cats were carried cff there will be some difficulty ;n procuring a sample of the complaint. However, doubtless this enterprising Australian knows best,and we cannot but admit that a disease which is capablelof carryine off cats so thoroughly must be a fairly cempetent one. Speaking of cats,l have lately inspected a truly wondrous device, consisting of this particular animal made of sheet iron, which it is possible to set. in motion by means of clockwork. The figure is intended to be placed on the roof of a house,a sheil,or back wall, in places where the night is made hideons by miaouvr- ings and caterwaulings. At the slightest touch or inter- ference,the clockwork sets the claws going all at once at a tremendous rate and there is temporary rest for the weary. EGG Sasesee, for a picnic makes a pleasant change, and can be easily carried by wrapping each egg in oiled paper, such as confectioners use. Boil six eggs, until quite hard and when celd remove the shells, cut the eggs in half, remove the yolks, and lay the whites aside. Mash the Nolke add a pinch of salt, a little pepper, one teaspoonful of olive oil, a little mustard, and a sprinkle of nutmeg. Then with two teaspoonfuls of vinegar stir this all together, replace in the whites and serve on lettuce. - .

SPINACH CUSTARD is delicious. Put a tablespoonful of cooked and sieved spinach in a bowl with a tablespoon- ful f milk, the strained yolk of an egg and a little seasoning. Mix all well together. Fill a,small buttered mould with the spinach, cover with buttered piper and set it in a saucepan of water that should be kept jugt simmering, tb- water to come about half-way up the mould. Cook till firm, and turn out very carefully.

• . The two LeNoirs simultaneously sprang forward, astonis!iment, diappointment and rage contending in their Olanched faces ?
"Who arc you, girl ?' exclaimed Colonel Le Noir.

"Capitola Black, yeur honour's glory!' she re- plied, making a deep courtesy. " What the foul fiend is the meaning of all this ?" in the same breath inquired the father and son. Cap put her thumb to the side of her nose and whirling her four ringers, replied : "It means, your worships' excellencies, that— you—can't—come it ! it's no go! this chicken won't fight. It means that the fat's in the tire and the cat's out of the bag. It.meaus confusion ! distrac- tion ! perdition ! and a tearing off of our wigs ! It means the game's up, the play's over, villiany is about to be hanged, and virtue about to be re- warded, and the curtain is going to drop and the principal performer—that's I—is going to be called out amid the applause of the audience?" Then suddenly changing her mocking tone to one of great severity, ,he said : "It means that you have been outwitted by a girl; it means that your proposed victim has fled, and is by this time in safety. It means that yol two, precious father and son would be a pair of knaves if you had sense enough; but, failing in that, you are only a pair of fools." By this time the attention of the few persons in the church was aroused. They all arose to their feet to look and listen, and some of them left their places and approached the altar. And to these latter Capitols now 'suddenly turned and said, aloud: "Good pe,ple, I am Capitols Black, the niece and ward of Major Ira. Wartield, of Hurricane Frail, whom you all knew; and now I claim your protection while I shall tell you the meaning of my presence here." "Don't listen to her I she is a maniac I" cried Colonel Le Noir. "Stop her mouth l" cried Craven, springing upon Capitola, and holding her tightly in the grasp of his right arm, while he covered her lips and nostrils with his large left hand. Capitols struggled so fiercely to free herself that Craven had enough to do to hold her, and so was not aware of a ringing footstep coming up the aisle, until a stunning blow dealt from a strong arm covered his face with blood, and stretched him out at Capitola's feet. Cap flushed, breathless, and confused looked tip, and was caught to the bosom of Herbert Greyson, who, pale with concentrated rage, held her closely and inquired: "Capitols, what violence is this which has been done you ?—Explain, who is the aggressor?' " Wai—wai—wait until I get my breath ! there! that was good. That villain has all but strangled me to death. Oh, Herbert, I'm so de- lighted you've come! How is it that you always drop rightdown at the right time and on the right spot ?" said Cap, while gasping for breath. "I will tell you another time. Now I want an explanation." "Yes, Herbert I also wish to explain—not only to you, but to these gaping good people. Let me have a hearing?? said Cap. "She is mad—absolutely mad !" cried Colonel Le Noir, who was assisting his son to rise. "SILENCE, sin !' thundered Herbert Greyson, advancing towards him with uplifted and threat- ening hand. "Gentlemen, gentlemen! pray remember that you are within the walls of a church!" said the distressed priest. ' Craven, this is no place for us—let us go and pursue our fugitive ward," whispered Colonel Le Noir to his son. "We might as well; for it is clear that all is over here,'' replied Craven. And the two baffled villains turned to leave the place. But Herbert Greyson, speaking up, said: , "Good people! prevent the escape of those two men until we hear what this young lady has to say, that we may judge Whether to let them go or take them before a magistrate." The people flew to the doom and windows and secured them, and then surrounded the two Le Noirs who found themselves prisoners. 'Now, Capitola, tell us how it is that you are here ?" said Herbert Greyson. " Well that elder man," said Cap, "is the guar- dian of a young heiress, who was betrothed to a worthy young man, one Dr. Traverse Rocke." "My friend," interrupted Herbert. "Yes, Mr. Greyson, your friend. The engage- ment was approved by the young lady's father, who gave them his dying blessing. Nevertheless, in the face of all this, this 'guardian' here, ap- pointed by the Orphans' Court to take charge of the heiress and her fortune, undertakes, for his own ends, to compel the young lady to break her engagement and marry his own son. To drive her to this measure, he does no,, hesitate to use every species of cruelty. This night he was to have forced her to this altar. But in the interval, to- day, I chanced to visit her at the house where she was confined. Being informed my her of her dis- tressing.situation, and having no time to help her in any better way, I ju.t changed clothes with her. She escaped unsuspected in my dress. And those two heroes there, mistaking me for her, forced toe into a carriage and dragged me hither to be married against' my will. And instead of catching an heiress they caught a Tartar—that's all! And now, Her- bert, let the two poor wretches go hide their mortification, and do you tai;.; me home, for I am immensely tired of doing the sentimental, making speeches, and piling up the agonies." While Cap was delivering this long oration, the two Le Noirs had made several essays to interrupt and contradict her, but were effectually prevented by the people, whose sympathies were all with the speaker. Now, at Herbert Greyson's command, they released the culprits, who, threatening loudly, took their departure. Herbert then led Capitola out, and placed her upon her own pony Gyp, which to her unbounded astonishment she found there in charge of Wool, who was also mounted upon his on n hack. • Herbert Greyson threw himself into the saddle of a third horse, and the three took the road to Hurricane Hall. " And,now," said Capitola, as Herbert rode up to her side, "for mercy's sake tell me, before I go crazy with conjecture, how it happened that you (-heaped down from the sky at the very mornent and on the very spot where you were needed? and where did you light upon Wool and the horses?' " It is very simple when you come to understand it,' said Herbert, smiling. •• Ia the first place, you know I graduated at the last Commence- ment?' Yes" " Well, I have just received a lieutenant's com- mission in a regiment that is ordered to join Gen- eral Scott in Mexico." " Oh, erbert that is news. and I don't know whether to,be in despair or in eestacy said Cap, ready to laugh or cry as a feather's weight might tip the scales in which she balanced Herbert s new honours with his a,pproachigg perils. •• if there a any doubt about it, I decidedly re- commend the latter emotion !" said Herbert, laughing. "When do you go ?" inquired Cap. " Our regiment embarks for Baltimore on the first of next month. Meanwhile I got leave of absence to come and spend a week with my fri, nds at ho ne.'' "Oh, Herbert, I—l am in a quandary! But you have'nt told me yet how you happened to meet with Wool and to come here just in he nick of time.'

'6 lam just going to do so. Well, you see, Cap. itela, I came down in the stage to Tip Top, which I reached about three o'clock. And there I found Wool in the hands of the Philistines, suspected of being mad, from the manner in which he raved about losing sight of you. Well, of course, like a trite knight I delivered my lady's squire, com- forted and re-assured him, and made him mount hie own horse and ' take charge of yours. After which I mounted the beast that I had hired to cohvey me to Hurricane Hall, and we set off thither. I confess that I was excessively anxious on your account, for I could make nothing what- ever of Wool's wild story of your supposed meta- morrosis. I thought it best to make a circuit, and take the Hidden House in our course, to make some inquiries there as to what had really hap- pened. I had got a little bewildered between the dark night and the strange road and seeing the light in the church, I had just ridden up to iaquire my way, when to my astonishment I saw you within, before the altar, struggling in the grasp of that ruffian. And you know the rest. And now let us ride on qui,:kly, for I have a strong presenti- ment that Major Warfield is suffering the tortures of a lost soul through anxiety upon your account," concluded Herbert Greyson. "Please, Marse Herbert and Miss Cap, don't you tell mars° .nutfen 'tall 'bout my losin', sight of you" pleadel Wool. "We shall tell your old master all about it, Wool, for I would not have him miss the pleasure of hearing this adventure upon any account; but I promise to bear you harmless through it," said Herbert, as they galloped rapidly towards kome.

div.head: CAPITOLA THE MADCAP. BY MRS. E. D. E. N. SOUTHWORTH.
div.p: CAPITOLA THE MADCAP. BY MRS. E. D. E. N. SOUTHWORTH.
CHAPTER XL. CAP IN CAPTIVITY. "4 I lingered here and rescue planned
For Clara and for me." —Scow. Meanwhile how fared it with Capitola in the Hidden House?

"1 am in for it now !" said Cap, as she closed the door behind Clara; "1 am in for it now This is a jolly imprudent adventure! What will Wool do when he discovers that he has 'lost sight' of me? What will uncle say when he finds out what I've done? Whe—ew ! Uncle will explode ! I wonder if the walls at Hurricane Hall will be strong enough to stand it? Wool will go mad! I doubt if he will ever do a bit more good in this world !

"But above all, I wonder what the Le Noirs, father and son, *ILL say when they find that the heiress has flown, and a beggar,' as uncle flatters me by calling me, will be here in her place! Whe—ew—ew—ew ! There will be a tornado! Cap, child, they'll murder you that's just what they'll do! They'll kill and eat you, Cap, without any salt! or they may lock you up in the haunted room to live with the ghost, Cap, and that would be worse!

4. Hush! here comes Dorcas Knight! Now I must make believe I'm Clara, and do the senti- mental up brown!" concluded Capitola, as she seated herself near the door where she could be heard, and began to sob softly.
, Dorcas rapped. Cap sobbed in response.

"Are you coming to luncheon, Miss Day?" in- quired the woman. " Ee—hee F Ee—he!Ee—hee t Ido not want to eat," sobbed Cap, in a low and smothered voice. Any one would have thought she was drowned in tears.

"Very well—just as you like," said the woman, harshly, as she went away. "Well, I declare," laughed Cap, "I did that quite as well as an actress could r But now what am Ito do? How long can I keep this up? Heigh- ho I let the world slide!' I'll not reveal myself untilym driven to it, for when I do--Cap, child,

you'll get chawed right up ! ' _ A little later in the day Dorcas Knight came again, and rapped at the door.. Ee—ho.e. 1 Ee—hre Ee —hee ! sobbed Cap. " Miss Day, your cousin, Craven Le Noir, wishes to speak with you alone." " Ee —Ate! Ee —heel Ee —her:l I cannot see him,''

soh',ed Cap, in a low and suffocating voice. The woman went away, and Cap suffered no other interruption until six o'clock, when Dorcas Knight once more rapped, saying: "Miss Day, your uncle is at the front door with the carriave, and he wishes to know if you are ready to obey him." " Ee—hee Ee—hee Ee —hre!—te —te --tell him yes !" sobbed Cap, as if her heart would break. Tie woman went off with this answer, and Capito'a hastily enveloped her form in Clara's large black shawl, put on Clara s black bonnet, and tied her thick mourning veil closely over her "A pretty bridal dress this! but, however, I Suppose these men are no more particular about my costume than they are about their own con- duct," said Cap. She bad just drawn on her gloves when she heard the foots eps of two men approaching. They rapped at the door. " Come in," she sobbed, in a low, broken voice, that might have belonged to any girl in deep dis tress, and she put a white cambric handkerchief up to her eyes and drew her thick veil closely over her ace. The twO Le Noirs home liately entered the room. Craven approa died her, and whispered softly : " You will forgive me this, my share in these proceedings after a while, sweet Clara. The Sabino women did not love the Roman youth-3 the less that they were forcibly made wives by theta." "Ee ! Ee !" sobbed Cap, entirely concealing her face in her white cambric handkerchief under her impenetrable veil. " come, come ! we lose time," said the elder Le Noir. " Draw her arm within yours, Craven, and lead her out.' _ _ _ _

The young man did as he was directed, and led Cap from the room. It was now quite dark—the long dreary passage was only dimly lighted by a han4ing limp, so that with the care she took there was scarcely a possibility of Capitola's being dis- covered. They went on, Craven Le N4ir whis- pering hypocritical apologies, and Cap replying only by sobs. When they reached the outer door, they found close carriage drawn up before the house'. To this Cm a en Le Noir led Capita, la, placed her within and took the seat by her side. Colonel Le Noir. placed himself on the front seat opposite them, and-the'earriage was driven rapidly off.' .An hour's ride-brought the party to an 'obscure church in the depths of the forest, Avhiel 'Capitols recognised by the cross on its, top .to be a Roman Catholic Chapel. Here the„carriage drew nip.and the two •Le 'Noirs got out and assisted Capitols.to-alight.. _ They then led her into .the church, which was .dimly illumined by a pair of wax candles burning before the altar. A,prVst in his sacerdotal robes was in attendance. A few country people were Scattered thinly about among the pews at, their private devotions. Guarded by Craven Le Noir on the right, arta Colonel Le .Noir on the left. Ca,pitola Was marched up the aisle and placed .before tto a tar. Colonel Le Noir then went and spoke apart to , the officiating priest, saying, in a tone of dissatis- faction : "I told you sir, that as our bride was an orphan, recently bereaved, and still in deep mourning, !Ave wished the marriage .ceremony to be strictly pri- vate, and you gave me to understand, sir, that at this hour, the chapel was most likely to be vacant. Yet here I find half a score of people. How is

this ?"•• '- * "Sir," replied the priest; "it is true that at this hour of the evening, the chapel is most likely •to be vacant, but it is not therefore certain to be so nor did I promise as much. Our chapel is, as you know, open at all hours of the day and night, that all who please may come and pray. These people that you see are hardworking farm la- bourers, who have no time to come in the day, and who are now here to offer uP their evening :prayers and also, smile of them to examine their consciences preparatory to confession. They can certainly be no interruption to the ceremony. ' "Egad, -I don't know that," muttered Colonel Le Noirbetween his teeth. - As for Cap the si lit of other persons present in the chapel filled her heart with joy and exultation, inasmuch as it ens3red her final safety. And so she, just abandoned herself to the spirit of -frolic that possessed her, and anticipated with the keenest • relish the denouement of ber strange adventure. " Weil, what are;wo' waiting for? -Proceed, sir,; proceed,' said Colonel La Noir, as he took Cap by _the shoulders and placetther on the left side. of his son, while he himself stood behind ready give . the bride away. The ceremony immediately commenced. The prologue be zinnin,*--" Dearly Beloved, we are gathered together &e., &c., &e., was

read. The solemn exhorta•ion to the contracting parties. •commencing:--‘• I require and charge .ye both, aj ye shall answer in the dreadful thy of judgment when the secrets of all hearts shall be disclosed, that if either of you know any just, cause or im- pediment why ye may not be lawfully be :joined together" &e., &c., &c., followed. Capitola listened to all this with the deepest, attention, saying to herself-7" Well, I declare,. this gettinl married is really awfully interesting. If it were not for 'Herbert Grey Son, just let it go right straight on to the end, and Sec what would happen next." While Cap was nriking these mental comments the priest was asking the bridegroom: "Win, thou have this woman to be thy wedded wife,' &c., &C., "so long as ye both shall
live?' To which Craven Le Noir, in a sonorous voice responded: "I will.' " Indeed you will? We'll see that presently," said t.'ap to herself. The priest then turning towards the bride, in-
quired - "Wilt thou .have this man to be thy wedded husband,' &e., &e., so king as ye both shall live 2" .

To which the bride, throwing aside her 'veil, answered firmly : "No ! not if he , were the last man and I.the last woman on the face of the earth, and the human race we e about to become extinct, and the angel Gabriel came (town from above to ask it of me as a personal favour." The effect of this outburst, this revelation, this explosion' may be imagined but can never be adequately described,

They reached Hurricane Hall by eight o'clock, and in good time for supper. They found Old Hurricane storming all over the house, and order- ing everybody off the premises, in his fury of anxiety upon Capitola's account. But when the party arrived, surprise at seeing them in the com- pany of Herbert Greyson, quite revolutionised his mood, and forgetting to rage, he gave them all a hearty welcome. And when after supper was over, and they were all gathered around the comfortable fire-side, and Herbert related the adventures and feats of Cap- itola at the Hidden House, and in the Forest Chapel, the old man grasped the hand of his favourite, and with his stormy old eyes full of rain, said:

"You deserve to have been a man, Cap I Indeed you do, my girl !" That was his highest style of praise'. Then Herbert told his own little story of getting his commission and being ordered to Mexico. "God bless you, lad, and save you in the battle, and bring you home with victory I" was Old Hur- ricane's comment. Then seeing that the young people were quite worn out with fatigue, and feeling not averse to his own comfortable couch, Old Hurricane broke up the circle, and they all retired to rest.
(To be continued.)

div.head: LOOKING FROM THE LONELY ROCK.
div.p: LOOKING FROM THE LONELY ROCK.

The island of St. Paul is merely a great rock in the Southern Ocean. It is the top of a volcanic mountain. There are no means of sustaining life to be found on it. The nearest inhabited land is Australia or Africa. To that ugly and des( late refuge came a boat containing nine persons—two of them womez. They had food—on short allowance,for perhaps a week. In less than three days they were half insane from anxiety. Water,water water everywhere, but no help. On the fifth day, at dawn, a brig hove to off the island. They saw her. Shouting, praying,weeping, they shim bled to the beach and were rescued. It was one cbanc ein a hundred. I'll tell you why some other time.
But, alas ! isn't it as bad or even w3rse on land?

Look at the physical wrecks in homes, in hospitals, and answer me. One perishes of privation from shipwreck. A thousand perish of privation in the midst of plenty. It isn't food they long for, but power to use it—worst and deadliest of all wants.

"My food seemed to give me no strength," says one of this army of unf ortunates,"and as the hopeless,starv- ing days passed slowly by I grew weaker and weaker. By-and-by my legs trembled and bent under me, and I could no longer get about.

"The ailment which reduced me to this fearful condi- tion began in the spring of 1892. At first I hardly re- cognised it for what we commonly call a disease. I felt tired, heavy, and languid, as one often does on the ap- proach of warm weather. I fancied it would pass away, but it did rot. I lost my appetite, and only ate from habit and to keep me going. I had no pleasure in it,and no warmth or glow followed it,as happens always when one is well. No matter how light and simple the repast was, or how careful I had been to select things tha would not be apt to hurt me, the result was the same. No sooner had I swallowed it than my stomach was die- tressed, and my chest and sides full of pain. If you will allow me so to put it, my food appeared to strike back at me,as though I had no right to use it.
"There was a nasty hitter flavour in my mouth, more or less headache, and a kind of nervousness, which
was new in my experience, as it was depressing and
cheerless.

" Mune remedics failing to help me, I consulted a doctor, but his prescriptions benefited me no more than our domestic medi eines had done. My flesh and streugth grew less, and I felt like one who has missed his way and looks in vain for a guide to point the road home.
"Finally I commenced attending the Leamington Hospital, and continued to do so for twelve months, but
the treatment they cave me had no better effect than all

You can hardly understand how weary I got of taking drugs. I turned almost with loathing from every new dose—n3t because of the taste, but because they deceived my hopes ; they were of no use to me. " In this state I w 4.9, when in March, 1894, a friend urged me to try Mother Seigel's Syrup. On account of the very reasons I have mentioned, 1 hated to experi- ment with any more medicines. But I overcame this aversion (most fortunately for me) and got a bottle of Mother S iger3Syrup,from Mr Judd ,the chemist in Learn-
the rest.
ington, anl after taking it I felt a marked awl great im- provement. I hAd no pain after eating and my fond felt right, digested, and gave me strength. As I grew

stronger my nerves ceased to trouble me. I can only say that by the conlinued use of the Syrup I got better daily and was soon as vigorous and as well aiever. have had no relapse, and have every reason to think

my cure ape rmanent rne. You are welcome to publish my letter. (Signed) (Miss) Lucy Eden, Tachbrook, near Leamington, September 26:h, 295." We hope Miss Eden's recovery may indeed prove per- manent, and if it does she will find no words too strong when she speaks of the reinedy which wrought it. But oh, the vast multitude who still stand, like the ship- wrecked people on the island, looking for rescue !—vic- tims of that most obdurate, common and baneful of
diseases, chronic dyspepsia. It is for their sakes we print it. May it reach many of them!

LAST WEEK'S TRAFFIC. During the weck ended Friday, May 22, the number of sett-ening vessels arriving at and sailing from the nort of Manchester was 132, representing an aggregate net registerei .tonnage ~f 36,250 tons. Of this total 104 vessels of 19,735 tons were engaged in the coasting trade and 28 vessels of 16,515 tons in the foreign traffic. Large cargoes of timber were imported by the steamers Ragni, Cato, Gyda, and Isle of Jura from the arid b the sailing ships Norma and Shakes- peare from Mobile and Apalachicola. The efforts which are now heing made to divert the Irish cattle trade to the Ship Canal appear to be meeting with an encouraging ineaur of success, as during the past week a large hurriber of sheep, lambs and cattle were landed in Mac- cheater by the Dublin steamer Bear. Large cargoes of ge,l,ral merchandise were loaded during the week for th Rrszils. the Persian Gulf, and China by the steamers ,garth, Z,llu acid Niagehow.

div.head: REPORTER AT RA.GLAN.
div.p: A REPORTER AT RA.GLAN.

A REPORTER writes :—" I asked Mrs. Hickey if she had really experienced the extraordinary escape locally rumoured. She said it certainly was true." "Two years agu last August," she said, " after the birth of my ninth child, I was very weak, and could not get up my strength at all. I' could take no food ; it caused me such severe pain across the chest and over the shoulders. If I ate any vegetabl(s, especially, distensions followed which necessitated loosening my clothes. I got so ill that I was obliged to give up ley house work, go to bed, and call in medical assistance. "While I was in bed," she continued, "I read in the papers of some astonishing cures effected by a means quite unli.k? any ordinary medicine. I refer to Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People. I determined to try them. Far five or six days previously I could eat nothing, and the only thing I could take at all was soda water. I was offered beef tea, chicken broth, &c.,but I could retain nothing. I had only taken half of a box of Dr. Williams' Pink Pills when I felt better. I felt I could eat, and my daughter, who had come home to nurse me, made me some toast. I ate little at first, but gradually improved and could take other food, which, as I have said before, I previously could not keep on my stomach at all. People are surprised to see me looking so well again. They used to remark how worn and haggard I was. My. eyes were sunken, ray face pinched, and my hands— well, you could, so to speak, see through them." "And you hold that Dr. Williams' Pink Pills have brought about all this wonderful improvement ?" " Certainly ;it could be nothing else. Before I took them I could take no food ; after I took them, I re- covered my appetite and regained my strength." Mrs. Hickey (whose address is Gnat Oak, Bryngwyn, 2-) near Raglan) added that ber husband 40 been benefited by taking Dr. Williams' Pink Pills whe feeling a bit run down and below par.

She said that everyone suffering in any way from lowness of spirits, hysteria,indigestion, and similar com- plaints should certainly try , Dr. Williams' Pills. Dr. Williams' Pills have cured numerous cases of paralysis, locomotor ataxy, rheumatism, and sciatica ;- also of all diseases arising from impoverishment and vitiated humours of the blood, which cause scrofula, rickets, chronic erysipelas, consumption of the bowels and lusgs aniemia, pale and sallow complexion, general muscula r weakness, loss of appetite,palpitation,pains in the back, nervous headache, early decay,all female weakness, and hysteria. These Pills are genuine only with the full name, Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People, and are sold by chemists and by Dr. Williams' Medicine Com- pany, 46, Holborn-viaduct, London, 8.C., at 2s. 91 a box, or six for 134. 9d. They are not purgative, but are unrivalled as a tonic for both sexes.

div.head: WYCLIFFE P.S.A,. SOCIFaY.
div.p: WYCLIFFE P.S.A,. SOCIFaY.

In Wycliffe Hall on Friday night,the annual meeting of the Wycliffe P.S.A. Society was held, when, several re- ports on the work of the society during the past year were submitted, and thelannual elect'on;of officers took place. The chair was occupied by Mr. James Haynes, and amongst those present were—Messrs. G. J. Brow.;, T. Winskill, W. H. Wallington, C. H. Mills, R. Atkin- son, T. Wallington' G. Wallington, Haley, R. Mills, Haviour, Cwen, and A. Lang. THE SECRETARY'S REPORT.

Mr. THOMAS WALLINGTON in subinitting his annual report said whije he could not lay-before them anything exceptional connected with the work of the society dur- ing the past twelve'months, he thought they could all look back again with thankfulness and satisfaction upon another year's steady and earnest labour. (Hear, hear.) There was no doubt that the year just closed was a severe testing time for all such movements as theirs, yet the interest in its meetings never flagged, and the at- tractive power which ushered in the existence of the society three years ago had been maintained and its great influence and moving spirit were felt as strong to- day as in the earlier days of the society's existence. The year closed with a subscribing membership of 1,161, and while that number showed a decrease of 42 com- pared with the previous year, it must not be taken as any indication whatever of declining interest or a waning enthusiasm'. For although the actual enrolled membership had been 42 less, the attendance at the meetings had been exceedingly good and as inspiring as heretofore. The approximated weekly average attend- ance at all the meetings of members and non-members had been 753, an estimated attendance more under than over the exact number present, which must be acknow- ledged to he highly satisf ctory and full of encourage- ment. At the end of the first six months of the year there were 5E5 books gained as prizes, and at the close of the last six months 684, making a total for the year of 1.269. It was worthy of notice that three-fourths of the looks gained were those of the first class. During the three years of the society'a existence the total num- ber of books distributed was 3,623—a result speaking for itself of strong attachments and deep interest exhi- bited by all the members, and carrying with it lasting and never-to-be-forgotten memories. During the same period over 500 certificates of merit had been ob- tained far regular and punctual attendance. At the -end of the first half of the year, a special' effort was made to re-awaken interest in the town an the society's behalf. This was done during the last week of August by canvassing the town, with the result that on the first Sunday in September 87 new members joined the society and that number had ,gone on increasing ever since. The Young Men's Bible Class still continued to gather within its circle many P.S.A. members not connected with other schools or churches. The finances of the society were-still in a very sound condition for after pay- ing all expenses and contributing to the church main- tenance fund there was a balance to carry forward again to the present year. The sick and absentee visi- tors had had another year of busy and active work and had very diligently and faithfully discharged their duties, and undoubtedly helping to a very large extent to keep up the interest in the society and main- taining that touch of brotherly sympathy so essential in movements like theirs. The Benevolent Fund Com- mittee had again done excellent work and had been in- etrumental 'in imparting cheer and com:ort to many hearts and homes. During the year the Temperance Pledge Committee decided to inaugurate a Total Abstin- ence Society which ccmmenced its meetings in a very promising way, but for several reasons it had had to be abandoned for the present, but with the hope of re- organising the movement at some future date. They were again much indebted to all who had made their meetings so joyous, happy and profit- able. Be would like to draw the attention of the members to the fact that books were given as special prizes for bringing new members, and he hoped many would go " missionising" for the society so that their members mieht be constantly increased. They had now entered upon their fourth year, and as they were thinking of the past let them "Thank God and take courage" and look with renewed confidence and hope to the future, for there was vet mach to be done. There was a wide field all around and they had glorious opportunities for service. (Applause.) The report was adopted. and it was ordered to be printed in the P.S.A. Year Bonk. * THE VISITING COMMITTEE.

MT. RICHARD MifAs submitted the report of the absentee visiting committee which showed that 1.075 visits had been paid by the members of the committee, and that they received 675 promises from members to attend. He pointed out that some of the absentee mem- bers had been visited two, three and four times so that the figures did not represent the nmnber of absentees.— The report was adopted on the motion of Mr. Brown.

div.head: TOTAL ABSTINENCE.
div.p: TOTAL ABSTINENCE.

Mr. C. H. Mims -spoke of the work of the Total Ab- stinence Society, and remarked that the drink traffic was the 2reatest curse, not only to their church but to their P.S.A.,and affected some of the members.—Mr. A. 'Tones also spoke on the work done during the yeor, and alluded to the financial position of the Society.

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.

Mr. R. Atkinson submitted the annual financial state- ment for the year ending February 23rd, 1896. It showed that the Tear commenced with a balance in hand of £6 17s. 81. The collections at the open meet- ings were £lB 17s. 81. : for Sunday sr•hool £7 16s ; members 'weekly subscription £l4O 174. 71. other sources £25 i. BJ., making a total of £199 103. 51 After meeting all expenses there was a balance carried for- ward of £3 12i. 7d. Mr. WINSKILL proposed that the balance sheet be adopted, and this was carried unanimously. THE BENFVOLRNT FUND.

Mr. A. LANG ie—aTd the report of .the Benevolent Fund which showed that the total amonnt collected from the boxes placed at thP d"ors was £l7 is. 60. The dis- bursements were £lO 183. 31. leaving a balance in hand of ..z.;6 34. Md. The report was adopted on the proposi- tion of Mr. %V. H. Wallington. ELECTION OF OFFICERS.

Mr. W. H. W-AlTin-gto-n propod, and Mr. Brown seconded, the re-election of the Rev. John Yonge as president. The resolution was carried unanim- nnslV. 'the following electi4ns were also m'ide :—General secretary, Mr. Thomas Wal- lington ; treasurer. Mr. R. Atkinson ; registra- tion secretarv, Mr. A. Knowles ; absentee visitors' see- Lang; benevolent tarY, Mr. Mills ; benevolent fund speretary ; Mr. A fund treasurer. gr. William Hick- man ; markers' secretary, Mr. W. Hayes ; steward's secretary Mr. J. Knowles, jun. choir leader and musical, director, Mr. W. 'H. Wallington ; total abstinence society secretaries, Messrs. and A. Jones. Votes of thanks concluded the meeting.

div.head: WARRINGTON BANKRUPTCY COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON BANKRUPTCY COURT.
FRlDAY.—Before Mr. Registrar Ridgway.

AN EARLESTOWN FANCY DEALER'S BANKRUPTCY.— Thomas Rudd, 30, Bridge-street, Earlestown came. up for his first public examination, in bankruptcy, by Mr. Potter.—Mr. Longton, solicitor, represented the debtor. The lsankrupt stated that he commenced business, as a fancy dealer about June, 1890, with £5O capital. He accounted for his deficiency, in part, as follows :—Bad debts, £l7 lls. 11d.; anticipated loss on forced realisa- tion of assets £lO6 155.; estimated loss in connection with a life policy, £2O : as to the balance he said that he did not file a deficiency account, based on a profit and loss accountos he had not kept proper books ; nor could fie explain how the remainder of his deficiency had arisen. The bankrupt furth r stated that he h.. d kept a cash receipts book,but only from 22nd April, 1893,and a cash payments book, but only from October, 1894,and that recording payments to creditors for goods only; that his books were never balanced ; and did not at any time within the past three years disclose his financial position. He alleged he first became aware of his in- solvency at Christmas, 1895; and admitted that he had contracted debts since that time which were still owing.' but he had paid off more debts than be had contracted since last year. The unsecured liabilities were £4O, for money lent; and as to the balance. for goods, &e. He also stated that he ran up most of his liabilities at the time of the coal strike. He could not say why he did not take the trouble to keep the record of accounts before April, 1893. He admitted that his books did not 'contain a record of every payment he'had received. Be never attempted t ascertain his financial position witn- in the past three years.—Mr. Potter said he was willing that the examination should be closed provided that the debtor's statement with regard to one account at St. Helens was corroborated within the next few days. BANKRUPTCY OF A WARRINGTON MONUMENTAL MASON. —Henry Srreete, Essenhigh, residing at 87, Manches- ter-road, Warrington, and formerly carrying on busi- ness at Manchester-road as a monumental mason, ap- peared for his first public examinatioa in bankruptcy. Mr. A. Brost ne,'solicitor, representbd the debtor. 'Che bankrupt alleged as the cause of his failure, bad trade, the purchase of had'material, taking over the liabili- ties of the firm of Essenhigh Bros., and making an allowance of 10s. a week to his mother. Be 54 Id he commenced business in 1883, in partnership with his brother, Frederick Arthur Essen- high,under the style of Essenhigh Brothers,as monumen- tal masons in Manchester-road. Wsrringten. Neither of them had any capital. About 1890 they dissolved part- neiship,and his brother retired from the business. sv6icti was then insolvent, the liabilities being about £350, and the assets ahout £5O. All the partnership liabilities were paid off long age.- He continued to carry on the business in his own name, his wife finding him money out of her separate estate. On March 19th.1894, he ex- ecuted a deed of assignment for the benefit of his credi- tors,in favour of C. R. Adamson, who sold the business to his wife for £3O odd. He had since been in her em- ployment. The liabilities under the deed were £l5O, and a dividend of 2s. 3d. in the £ had been dsclaree. The tankrupt had not filed the prescribed deficiency ac- crunt. He said his deficiency arose owing to his expen- diture exceeding his income. As he had not kept books, he could not file a proper deficiency account. He lost money through having bad stone sent to him, end through taking over his brother's liabilities, and paying for the support of his mother. fTe alleged he first be- came aware of his insolvency in 1893, and that he had not contracted any debts with such knowledge. The unsecured liabilities were wholly for atone. With regard to assets the banbrupt stated that his wife was the ten-

ant of the dwelling-fiouse and business premises. The household furniture, .the business which he formerly carried on.ancl some money in the Starr Bowkett-Build- log Society belonged t 3 her. He farther stated that he was married in July, 1884. She then had about £l2O of her own. She also inherited £235 from her mother,and £3OO from her sister. Ile at first refused the bad stone which was sent' for hina and it lay at the station fcr some months. The merehant afterwards
came over and be (Mr. Essenhigh) paid him £25 for it subject to deductions. The merchant never made de- ductions and sent him a writ for the full amount. The _ _

stone was rubbish and unfit for use.—ln cross-examina- tion by Mr. Browne.the debtor stated that he could not afford to go to•Sheffi,,ld and oppose the account for the stone.—The examination was closed.

div.head: TRAINING FOR THlii MILITA.RY TOURNAMENT.
div.p: TRAINING FOR THlii MILITA.RY TOURNAMENT.

"To many who each year look forward with pleasur- able anticipations to the Military Tournament, it may be of interest," writes Mr. Ernest W. Low, in the May number of the " Windsor Magazine," to learn some- thing about the system which brings about such a pitch of excellence as is therein displayed. " The sergeant who,when sitting for his education certificate,wrote that Canterbury was famous for its riding schools was per- haps a poor historian but a very typical cavalry man. The Establishment, or—to give it the name by which it is generally known—tha "Stab," is virtually the cavalryman's university. And as such it is regarded throughout that arm of the service. The very first thing the men have to do on joining their class is to go through a preliminary gymnastic course, which maiuly, consists of a series of evolutions on a wooden horse for the purpose of attaining facility at mounting and dismounting without the aid of stirrups. By this means a certain degree of flexibility and agility is achieved and the men are preparing them- selves for the barebacked course which follows. Many people will remember the excellent performance of this kind at the last Tournament; the men engaged in it were from the establishment, at which it forms part' of the regular training. "For this purpose the horse is equipped with a sort of girth or surcingle, attached to the top of which are two handles for the • man to hold when he vaults on its back. It is quite astonishing to see what a degree of proficiency the men reach in this work ; they mount and dismount while the horse is at a swinging canter, ride face to tail' and even go over jumps in that awkward position. Every man has to break the horse which is to carry him through his course, and a very ticklish busi- ness it sometimes is. The remounts are usually four-year olds, and are mostly bred in Ireland; The majority of them have never had a bridle in their mouths, and it is by no means unusual for a spirited yongster to show his very decided objection to being subjected to• that badge of servitude; and the an- tics of a young horse are not altogether amus ing when you happen to be on his back. "Of course very great care has to be taken, as rough treat- ment might spoil the prospect of the iemount develop- ing into a reliable troop-horse. His mouth may easily be ruined by awkward handling, and it is for this very re,kson that the training of a young horse forms part of the curriculum. Until their horses are fairly well broken in, the class devotes its energies mainly to that task. Not only has the remount to be schooled to obey the bit and leg, but he has to get used to the flash of the sword and the firing of a carbine. When the preliminary part of the horse's education is accomplished the men begin to take them through the more complex evolutions, to which the pub- lie have become fairiiliarised by means of the Toarna- ment. And here again it is a very mistaken idea to suppose that these movements are simply of use for show purposes. Experience has shown that by making a horse perform certain figures the process of training , him to obey the slightest touch of rein and spur, or, as it is technically styled. ' bending' him, is greatly facil- itated. Thus the majority of. the movements in the double ride, though they may appear to the uninitiated but fantastic devices, are in reality important factors in the work of horse-breaking."

div.head: NONCONFORMISTS AND THE I RISII
div.p: NONCONFORMISTS AND THE I RISII
PARTY.

The "Westminster Gazette" says:—"WE telegraphed to Mr. Gladstone; at Hawarden, this morning, to ask if we tnight say int:thing en his behalf ino reply to the , threats of are Nonconformist leaders and newspapers that they would abandon Home Rule in consequence of the action of the Irish members on the Education Bill. Mr. Gladstone has replied to us as follows :—' I am in- disposed ta interfere as lam unable to take part with either Fide.—W E, GLADSTONE.' ID view of the serious development of the split be- tween the English Nonconformists and the Irish Nationa- lists, as disclosed by the articles in the " Methodist Times" and the "British Weekly," the Editor of "The Daity Chronicle" addressed the following telegram to I Mr. Gladstone :—" Prominent .Nonvriformists papers like the "Methodist Times" and the "British Weekly" declare that Home Rule is dead, and we are receiving many Nonconformist letters in this sense, based on the Irish vote on the Education Bill. Our opinion is strong that the argument for Home Rule, based on British honour and Imperial interests, is absolutely unaffected. Will you confirm this ? " To this communication Mr. Gladstone was good enough to address' the following reply • Cannot appear in the matter, but agree with I Editor. Blame Irish a little, Nonconformists more, Parnellites by far the most."

div.head: "CAPITAL" CHAT.
div.p: "CAPITAL" CHAT.

When members return to the House of Commons after the holidays,and take their lady friends down to tea on the terrace overlooking the river,they will find another innovation on the old exclusive tradi- tions of Parliament. The tea and cake or straw- berries and cream will no longer be served out by professional waiters as heretotore,but by a dozen or twenty waitresses. in neat and attractive uniform. Young ladies have already been allowed to serve at some of the refreshment bars inside the House, but their appearance on the terrace in a business capa- city is a distinct encroachment on the province of the male. The elderly fogies of the House resent the introduction,and make gloomy forecasts of the time when women.will not only be seated on the benches of the House itself, but on the Treasury Bench, and even in the Speaker's chair. Sufficient, however, for the day is the evil thereof, and in the meantime the first problem will be whether the young ladies whose functions now lie on the ter- race will not soon be sent to the hospital in swarms, victims of the cold piercing east winds which at this season of the year blow with deadly chill up the river, and sometimes make a thick wrap wel- come.

The • metropolitan volunteers have spent their Whitsuntide holidays in getting through a modest and fair ambiint of instructive work. There were no manceuvres on a great scale, but all round Lon- ' don for many miles brigades have been at work perfecting themselves in some branch or other of military drill with the most commendable assiduity. Detachments numbering several thousands com- peted for prizes at Bisley, and as a good many cups were to be shot for, some honours worth having were carried off A great deal of attention was given in some brigades to signalling. The West London brigade gave itself up vigorously to long- distance signalling, and besides appl3ing the whole.of Whit-Monday to the work, they indented largely upon Sunday afternoon and evening.. The heliograph and large flags and small formed means of practice by day, and lamps Were used well into the night for flashing night signals.— The artillery volunteers were again at Shoeburyness and Sheer- ness, in both of which places some excellent gun practice was obtained. Most of the volunteers are in training again to-day, and all are returning to London to-night.

The Bank Holiday has come and gone,and labour for the most part has returned to its workshop, its stall, and its desk, refreshed by the day's cessation from toil and the splendid weather. What ispecu- liar in connection with the present holiday is the fact that the metropolitan holiday-makers atJeast have not gone so far afield as they have been gener- ally in the habit of doing. There have been fewer visitors to remote localities than in recent years,but on the other hand the points of attraction within easy reach of the metropolis have been more fre- quented. Whether this, is a merely accidental circumstance, or has same deep-seated cause in connection with family economies, it is impossible to say. But at this season the attractions within a few miles of the metropolis are very great. The railway and steamboat returns no longer furnish us with a criterion of the number who spend their holiday in the country, for the bicycle now carries off both men and women by tens ot thousands by every avenue that leads from London. Thus some of the most beautiful places within 30 miles of the metropolis, which were scarcely even known geographically a few years ago, are familiar Vaunts of members of nearly every family. The bicycle is responsible for conveying out of town nearly as many pleasure-seekers as some of the more,favoured railways. •

One consolation which Liberals have found in their exclusion from office has been a sort of quiet satisfaction that on their opponents has fallen the necessity of dealing with the luxuriant crop of foreign and colonial difficulties which have followed upon the heels of their administration. But those who look further into the causes of things have long been of opinion that there would never have been any conspiracy against the Transvaal, with its accompaniment of the Jameson raid, but for the English general election of last July. The further telegrams that are coming to hand largely bear out the belief that the plotters reckoned on a very blind eye being turned on their proceedings by a Con- servaAve Government credited with a continued hatred of the policy which followed upon Majuba Hill.

It is evident that Mr. Cecil Rhodes is a great be- liever in the policy of forcing the hands of sympa- thetic Governments, and is willing enough to un- dergo the farce of momentary censure whic% the calculates on being followed by calm acceptance of the fruits of the wrong-doing. He is thoroughly imbued with the prancing pro-consul theory. Its regards the Imperial Government, as at present constituted, as willing to profit by the stolen goods against whose conveyance it hypocritically pro- tests. His anger at English officers not seizing a fort on the hill, while assured lf open censure and secret approval, is indicative of this. So, too. the assurance of one of his friends that formal official blame of the Jameson business would be only part of the game by a Pecksniffian Government, only too glad to see the retrocession of the Transvaal and its restoration to the Boers wiped out.

I bear that the Czar's manifesto is regarded most unfavourably among the Russian exiles and" friends of Russian freedom." Of course the political refugees have never for a moment expected any amnesty to cover their own cases. But the expect- ation, for instance, that corporal punishment would be finolly abolished was practically universal in Russian society, which had been much moved in this point by the recent vigorous appeals of Count Leo Tolstoi and other leading writers. That a Cor- onation manifesto should have been issued without a reference to this matter, and without a word as to education and the censorship—to say nothing of the abolition of administrative punishment, religious toleration, prison reforms, and the beginnings of representative government—is regarded as a por- tentous sign. A document so utterly barren had not, been expected; and it is considered certain that the effedt of this uncompromising denial of every request to the Russian Liberals will have an immediate and possibly serious effect upon the internal situation of the Empire. It cannot but stimulate those extreme political sections which have, so far, been kept quiescent by the hope of a new regime.

There is excellent authority for stating that the French Ambassadors to the Powers have been in- structed to open negotiations with the Govern- ments to which they are accredited on the subject of the future government of the. Asian provinces of Turkey. The massacre in Crete will, of course, have the effect of ren4ering these negotiations op- portune. My authority adds: "You my take it for granted that M. klanotaux proposes to win laurels from the Eastern Question, and in a manner which will be a surprise to theldiplomacy of the Triple Alliance."

The disgust with which Ministerialiats contem- plate the prospects of the Education Bill increases day by day. There is a good deal of whistling to keep up their courage, but this fails to conceal their evident belief that closuring by compartments is the only means by which the Bill can be got through, and it is equally evident that this is an "odious device" which the more level-headed among them regard as a greater evil than the lose of a large part or the Bill. The difficulties of the situation from the Government point of view are increased by the fact that, a very considerable pro- ' portion of the amendments come from the Minis- terial side of the house. The Marquis of Lorne has been racking his brain to devise methods by which these dissatisfied ones may consolidate their pres- sure and restrict it to the particular point. But hopefulness in he possibility of his project indi- dates an ingenuousness ot mind and an inexperi- ence Gf the vagaries of human nature which are more charming than practical. This is, indeed, already told by his own friends, 01-at his notion of concentrating attention on one principle is open to the fatal objection that the principle he advocates is not at present within the four corners of the Bill.

Mr. Balfour's arbitrariness last Thursday night had two wholesome effects. It angered the Opposi- tion because of its contemptuous unfairness to them and its disreTect to the Constitution, and while angering them it also gave them proof of their strength. It showed them how much even a small minority can do when acting in unison, and what- ever divergencies there may be on the Education Bill as a whole, in all matters affecting the c103ur,3 the Irish members may. be counted upon to go solid for the Liberals.

Mathews, Father Moore, and J. H. Riddette, Messrs. A. J. Jolley, A. Jolley, G. Thomp- son, T. B. Malkin W. Hickman,W. Houghton, J.Clarke, J. Billinge, T. Ha!lton, J. Johnson, and J. C. div.head: FREE CHURCH COUNCIL.
div.p: THE FREE CHURCH COUNCIL.

- The House Committeu's minutes stated that Mr. A. J. Jolley had been appointed chairman, and Mr. A. Jolley vice-chairman for the ensuing year. The committee alSo recommended that the Tuesday night services which had been held and conducted ny members of the Free Church Council, and which were allowed for three months, be further extended, and that the tanks of the Committee be returned to the Free Church Council.— Mr. A. J. Jolley in moving the adoption of the Commit- tee's minutes said from time to time questions had been brought before them by the Free Church Council, some of which he had been strongly opposed to. But it gave ' him pleasure to bear the testimony of the master and matron that the services had been very successful. He 'thought the Guardians ought to feel grateful to the Free Church Council for what they had done.—Rev. J. H. Rtddette said he was sorry their friend,Mr.Knowles,was not present. (Laughter.)—Mr. Thompson seconded the adoption of the minutes, and referring to the gift of flowers by the Wesleyans of Padgate, said be believed if the public only knew that the flowers were a great boon to the inmates of the hospital, the institution would receive a great many more than was the case at present. It would be a great charity on the part of those who had flowers spoiling in their garden if they would send a basket of them to the institution for the benefit of the inmates. (Hear, hear.)—The minutes were carried.

div.head: PADGATE SCHOOLS.
div.p: PADGATE SCHOOLS.

The minutes of the Padgate Schools Committee stated that the committee approved of an advertisement drawn up by the Clerk for superintendent, schoolmaster and matron of Padgate schools, and that a special committee meeting be held at the Clerk's office on June 2nd, at'two o'clock, to consider the testimonials and select candid- ates to appear before the Board. The committee also resolved that for the present no girls should go out for service.—Referring to the appointment for Padgate schools, the Clerk said according to the number of applications which, he understood, exceeded fifty, it would be a difficult matter t 2 go through the applications at his office. The committee censisted of over twenty members and there would be about 300 documents to go through. He therefore asked the members to hold the meeting in the Board-room and to meet at ten o'clock in the morning instead of two o'clock in the afternoon as proposed. There was no need of hurrying the appoint- ment. The superintendent and the matron were quite willing to stay until the Guardians said they should go. It was necessary for financial reasons that they should continue until the end of the financial year, and it was also desirable on account of the annual treat, and their familiarity with past arrangements in connection with it and the band. He would suggest that the applications should remain open for a con- venient period for the inspection of the Guardians.— The Rev. J. Fl. Riddette thought it would be prolong- ing the agony of the applicants. He did not think any advantage would arise from such a course. He would like to know how long they would have to wait after the date of the committee's selections before the candidates appeared before the 83ard.—The Clerk said it would re- main with the members whether they decided the mat- ter a fortnight from that date or deferreckit for a month. —Mr. A. J. Jolley said he dissented from the Clerk's idea that there was no necess;ty for hurrying the mat- ter on. He thought the sooner it was done the better. (Hear, hear.) ft was ultimately decided that the com- mittee should consider the applications at the Board- room on June 2nd, and that the Board should make the appointment at their next meeting.—Mr. Thompson said he would like to propose that the Rev. Father Moore be added to the Committee for Padgate Schools. —This was unanimously agreed to.—The Rev. Father Moore accepted the pcsition and said it was well kn )wn that he had not exactly killed himself with work on the committee in the past but he hoped to make up for it in the future. (Laughter.) On being permitted to make a few remarks by way of a personal explanation, he said they were all agreed that there was no strict necessity for the direct representation of reli- gious interests on that Board. He (Father Moore) was the only Roman Catholic on the Board and it had been stated that he did not do as much in pushing Catholic cl iims as he might do. But the last thing he would think of being would be that of a trimmer. If he had been returned by a Catholic vote he should have voted on every reasonable occasion for what he eonsidered to be in the interests of • the denomination to which he be- longed. But he had no such mandate. He was returned by a meeting of non-Roman catholics. When it was too late for him to withdraw it was said that he (Father Moore) was a man of fair promises, but now that he was returned, the church people and Dissenters might fish for his support. It was in consequence of this state of affairs that he had placed himself in the position he had done. In his opinion there was nothing in connection with that Board to raise a row about. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) He felt perfectly certain that whatever his (the Roman catholic) people were entitled to, there was no disposition on the part of the Board to keep it from them. If there waez, he should do his best to get it for them. Some people had told him that there was a sus- eicion that he had been illtreated when he severed his connection with the Padgate Schools Committee. He advised them to disbelieve anything of the sort, He did not know whether his connection with that Board would he long or short hut he should carry away with, him feelings of gratitude and friendship to every member of that Board. (Hear, hear.) The Rev. J. H. Rildette : What a pity it is that Mr. Knowles is not here. (Laugh- ter).

div.p: MILITARY INMATES
