He (the clerk) had received a communication from an official of the Registrar General stating that he was directed to state with reference to the present vacancy in the office of registrar of births and deaths for Latchford sub-district for the information of the Warrington Guardians, that the Registrar General pro- posed to take the present opport mity to make the fol- lowing changes in the situation of the subdistrict of the Warrington registration district, i.e., to add Latchford sub-district, which as now constituted was entirely within Warrington municipal borough. to Warrington sub-district, thus placing the whole of the Borough within one registration sub-district. (2) To transfer that part of the Winwick civil parish now formine, part of Warrington sub-district to IN inwick sub-district and (3) to transfer Little Sankey civil parish from Warring- ton sub-district to Sankey sub-district. It was pointed out that these changes would make Warrington sub-dis- trict co-extensive with the municipal borough which would obviously be desirable on many grounds. He , requested that before taking any steps to fill the present 1 vacancy in the office of registrar for Latchford sub-dis- trict, the Guardians would favour him with their obser- vations on the proposed changes.—The Clerk referred to the numerous changes which bad taken• place with reference to the Latchford district. The registrar general proposed to add it to the Warrington" district without having knowledge of the extension of the boundaries to the Ship Canal. He also proposed to add Little Sankey to Great Sankey, but by the extension bill Little Sankey would be within the Borough. If the proposed alterations were now made they would have to be broken again within a few months which would make confusion worse con- founded. He (Mr. Sutton) suggested that as The Chairman and himself were to be in London on the question of the bill now before Parliament, they should see the Registrer-General and explain the whole matter to him. He would be glad of an expression of opinion as to whether they desired Latchford district to be added to Warrington for the purposes of registration.— The Chairman said it would be to the advantage of mast people in Latchford that it should be kept a sepa- rate registration district.—Mr.Jolley also spoke in favour of Latchford remaining a separate registration district. —ln reply to Mr. Hickman as to what the area of Latch- ford would be, the Chairman said that owing te the Ex- tension Bill it would be a very large one extending to the Ship Canal, and including apa t of Appleton. It would be a vety long way from the Warrington regis- trar's office..—Mr. Thompson thought the matter might be left in the hands of the Chairman and the Clerk to arrange with the Registrar-General.—Mr. A. J. Jolley was of the opinion that the convenience of the public • would be met by making one district co-extensive with the borough.—lt was ultimately decided to let the Chair- man and the Clerk make the best arrangements they could with the registrar.

div.head: EDUCATION BILL.
div.p: THE EDUCATION BILL.

'I he CLERK read a communication from the Gateshead Union, in which attention was calla to clause 2, sub- clause 3of the Education Bill, which stated that" The Education Authority fez' a County shall act as and should be substituted for the School Attendance Committee for every school district in the county for which there is for the time being no school board and which is not a borough other than a county borough and the expehses of their so acting shall be a special expense chargeable exclusively to the parishes for which they so act." It was pointed out that there were 771 school attendance committees in England and Wales representing a pop- ulation of 9,243,092. As the total population of Englacd and Wales was 29,002,525 it would be seen that the change proposed was very great. In the opinion of the Gateshead Guardians no sufficient reasons had been given to justify the change, and they trusted that the Warrington Guardians would cause communications to be sent to their members of Parliament asking them to vote ,for the elimination of that clause from'the bill. —The Rev. J. .H. Riddette said he hoped the Clerk and Mr. Pilling would not vote in favour of the ' elimination of that clause if it was brought before the Poor Law Conference. He thought it would be a very great advantage if the work of the School Attendanze Committees was taken over by the Education Authority. —Mr. A. J. Jolley said he entirely dissented from the views of the Rev. J. H. Riddette. Although it had been proved that n some school attendance districts the work had been neglected, yet in a great many places it had been efficiently done. He did not think the Guar- dians had any reason to be ashamed of the work that had been done by the School Attendance Committee of that Union. (Hear, hear.) Personally, he viewed with considerable distrust the proposed new education authority and he vent red to think that if it was ap- pointed as suggested without some considerable altera- tion, their work and the Bill would prove a huge blun- der. (Hear, hear.)—The Chairman said he was exactly of the same opinion.—The Rev. J. H. Riadette said he preferred that the entire responsibility for the attend- ance should be handed over to the central 'authority.— The Clerk having painted out the mode of dealing with such resolutions at conferences, the subject dropped.

div.head: VOTE OF STAIPATIIY.
div.p: A VOTE OF STAIPATIIY.

Mr. THOMPSON said before they separated he thought it was only the wish of the members that tt:ey should send a vote of sympthy to Mr. Dignum in the bereave- ment of his wife. Mr. Dignom was a gentleman they all respected, and he was sore they all sympathised with him in the loss he had sustained. Be proposed that the Clerk write Mr. Dignum to that effect.—Mr. Halton seconded, and it was supported by Mr. Malkin and Mrs. Clay, and unanimously agreed to.

div.head: PADGATE RCHOOLS SPECIAL COMMITTEE.
div.p: PADGATE RCHOOLS SPECIAL COMMITTEE.

The Rev. J. H. RinnErrs asked whether the Special Committee had anything to report with reference to Padgate Schools.—The Clerk said there was nothing ex- cept that Mr. Mines' resignation was accepted, and that it was decided to advertise, and make another appoint- ment.—The Rev. J. H. Riddette said he would like to know whether the superintendent had applied for a retiring allowance.—The Clerk said that could not be made until the completion of his services. He (the Clerk) had written to the Local Government Board and explained the whole matter to them.—The Chairman said that matter would come befOre them in due time. This concluded the business.

div.head: CHURCH AND THE ARMY IN
div.p: THE CHURCH AND THE ARMY IN
JAPAN.
A DEPUTATION TO STUDY THE RUSSIAN SYbTEDd.

The "Times of India " says :—" AccustoMed as we are in Bombay to an endless variety of costume, it has not escaped attention that there are now three Japanese Buddhist priests in this city on their way to Resole. At first it may seem difficult to imagine what possible interest Russia or Its people can have for the Buddhists of Japan, and, oddly enough, the visit is indirectly due to the recent war between J pan and China, the effects of which can only be fully appreciated by degrees. These Japanese priests are bent upon studying the details of the system under which the Church militant in Russia is affiliated to the army of the Czar. They consider that in no other country in the world does religion go so thoroughly hand-in-hand with war as in Russia, and there is special need in Japan of a modifica- tion of existing arrangements,for the recent war brought to light sad defects. There have never been any army chaplains attached to the Japanese forces,and wheethe late war broke out it was discovered that there was no provision for performance of th 3 last offices for those slain on the battlefields of Cnrea and Manchuria. The regulation ceremony of burial in the Japanese army is that of Shintoism (the beaetiful simplictty of which is very touching), but practically it is seldom performed in time of peace, for the relations of the deceased generally receive the body and observe the rites of their own creed. During the late war this was, of course, impossible, and t .e priests took the oppnrtunity di apply to the Army Department to be permitted to follow the forces. Their request was granted, and priests of every denomi- nation hastened to the fi 4(1. the first to embark being of that sect to which our present visitors belong. Their new experience warned them of the necessity of system- atic organisation aed of go ri management, and their preference has been given to Russia, for the reason that religion has so strong an iefluence in the army of that country. Our visitors are Ibiddhist Protestants, so re speak, a sect of comparatively modern origin. The priests of this sect are freo to eat fish and meats denied to other sects, and they also marry and succeed to pro- perty just like laymen. It was founded by Shin-ran Sho-nin about. 600 yeers aim. Their doctrine embodies the theory that the ordinary Buddhist priests of these degenerate days cannot attaim to the higher pasitions in Nirvana by their own deeds and exertions only, and are therefore powerless of themselves to save the seuls of others. And the eoDelusion is that conformity to strict religious practices,stp h as fasting. and orthodox ceremonies in general,tannnt he necessary to salvation, the repetition of a few simple words expressing faith in the Deity being cansidered sufficient. The founder did not himself claim to be a eriest,but regarded himself as a layman, in no way different from other people save that he went a step in advance of his fellows in search of truth,and considered it h's mission to place the know- ledge thus obtaine3 at the disposal of mankind. It will be easy to infer from this that the faith of these Budd- hist Protestants presents no impediments to the pefor- mance of mundane duties. 'Nis Elect is the richest in Japan.and has more adherents than any other. It lake its academy and nnrmel c liege. and sends Slnscrit students to Oxford Univers;te.lt has branches in Sheng- hai, the Corean ports, and Viedivostock for proselytis- ing. Our visitors are now waiting for a student of their sect who is coming from Ha neoon, where he has been studying Buddhism for sev,ral years, to join them, and they contemplate making a eilerimaee to Buddh Gaya oh their way to Russia. tle,is• route being overland to Moscow. via Afghanistan. PI is to be feared that their pathway will prove somewhat thorny."

Well, and what do they tell us. div.head: SA.TURDAY, MAX 30th, 1896.
div.p: SA.TURDAY, MAX 30th, 1896.

THE meeting of the Co-operative Co-epe eratorss s in Congress at Woolwich has been Congr. one of the leading events of the present week. The famous arsenal town is cer- tainly entitled to the honour which has been conferred upon it by the general body of co-opera- tors. Co-operation does not flourish in the South of England as it does in the North. It is said that amongst the vast population of the metropolitan district there are only four societies on the Roch- dale plan which have a membership of more than a thousand. The Royal Arsenal Co-operative Society is one of the four, and it is certainly a splendid exception to the general rule. This Society was founded as many flourishing co-opera- tive societies have been founded in the north of England, that is to say by the joining together of a few intelligent and energetic workingmen in order to buy and distribute commodities for their own use. The total capital of these few enterpris- ing artisans was £7 4s. 6d. That was in 1868 ;in 1896 the capital of the Society of which they were the originators is not less than £BO,OOO, and its membership numbers eight thousand. The origi- nal shop, in which the counter was a workman's bench, has been replaced by solid and capacious central premises with four flourishing branches, and amongst the other adjuncts of the Society are such things as a model bakery which cost £16,000, a palatial stable containing eighty horses and a fine library stored with 4,000 volumes. This Society has attempted, and evidently with a considerable amount of success to combine production with distribution. It has its own farm upon which it raises largo quantities of vegetables and fruit besides fattening the pork and producing the poultry and eggs which are sold in its own shops. So far this go-ahead Society seems to have prospered in all its branches, and it is hinted that its next enterprise will take the form of a scheme for utilising its surplus capital in help- ing its members to acquire their own houses. It will be seen, therefore, that Woolwich was fairly entitled to the honour of being selected as the meeting place of the Co-operative Union. The meeting was one of the largest, if not the largest, of these annual gatherings of co-operators which has yet been held. More than a thousand co-opera- tive societies in Great Brit lin and Ireland were invited to send representatives, and there were as a matter of fact between eight and nine hundred delegates present. The mere enumeration of these figures is sufficient to shovi the extraordin- ary growth which co-operation has made in recent years. The report of the Central Board states that there are now no fewer than 1,711 different co-operative societies, with a total membership of 1,414,158, doing an annual business of more than £52,502,126, and holding a capital of ove £16,000,000. T'lere was, too, abundant evidence furnished in the course of the Congress that co- operation is now utilised in ways which were scarcely thought of a few years ago. Lord WINCHELSEA, who gave the inaugural address, suggested the formation of a great co-operative society for the growth, collection, and distribution of British produce, the profits to be divided between producers and consumers. This scheme is as yet in a very nebulous condition, bat the mere mention of it by such a zealous agriculturist as Lord WINCHELSEA was in itself significant. A paper which was subsequently read at the Con- gress also went to prove that co-operative methods of production and distribution are being exten- sively adopted in other countries. A considerable proportion of the butter and cheese consumed in this country is prepared in co-operative creameries in Ireland, in Denmark, or even in far-away New Zealand; bacon is cured in co-operative factories, and numerous other commodities are either pro- duced or exchanged on co-operative lines. In almost every country, in fact, the cultivators of the soil are beginning to realise that union is strength and that it is to their advantage to buy and to sell co-operatively. There seems to be, in fact, in many industries and many countries a general movement in the direction of combination, and as long as this movement continues progress will be reported at every succeeding meeting of the Co-operative Union.
THE all-night sitting which took

The All-Night Sitting. place in the House of Commons at the end of last week has had two useful results. It has, in the first place, drawn the attention of the country to the real character of the Land Rating Bill with a com- pletenE•ss which could not have been effected by any other means. It has, in the second place, revived the spirits of the Opoosition to a remark- able extent. Mr. BALFOUR'S leadership of the House ef Commons has not at any time been con- spicuously successful ; in connection with this Rating Bill it has distinctly faded. It is not sur- prising that the Government should wish to push the Bill through with as little discussion as pos- sible, There is absolutely no defence for the pro-
posal to tax the whole of the population of these islands at the rate of a shilling per head for the sole

benefit of the landlords. The Government and their I followers know this—hence this indecent haste to closure debate. The all-night sitting was, there- fore, a timely reminder that even a comparatively weak opposition cannot be coerced beyond a cer- tain point. Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT has, of course, been severely blamed by the Tory news- papers and speakers for the part he has taken in opposing the Rating Bill, but Sir WILLIAM does not show any signs of repentence. He has, on the contrary, published a letter in which he vigor- ously condemns the methods of the Government, and points out the serious consequences that will result from the passing of the Rating Bill. At the first it was declared that the Bill was devised solely for the purpose of relieving agricultural distress, but when it was pointed out that a large part of the £2,000,000 would go to districts which did not require any relief, a change of front was made and it was as- sorted that the Bill was really for the reform of local rating quite irrespective of agricultural dis- tress. This, as Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT says, vastly increased the importance and complexity of the measure, by making it strike "root and branch" at the whole machine of local imperial finance. Yet Mr. BALFOUR as the spokesman of the Government would give no opportunity for considering and discussing the Bill from this new aspect, and most fair minded people will agree with Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT that it was then time" that this high-handed attempt to suppress discussion should be encountered by a firm and de- cisive resistance."

The Liberals are preparing in earnest to retain the seat vacated by Mr. Speakman on the Cheshire County Council. Mr. Norman the candidate selected is an excellent one, and as his views on the education question are distinctly progressive he will be of great use on a body which will accord- ing to the present prospects have greater power than eTer put into its hands.

Mr. Woodward atthe Runcorn Board of Guar- dians succeeded this week in getting hie resolution in favour of sending the children of the Workhouse to outside schools, confirmed almost unanimously. Arrangements will therefore be made for the carry- ing out of the terms of the resolution, and no doubt under the healthier outside influences the children will receive a better education and will in other ways be enabled to commence life better equipped than they otherwise would have been.
SIR JOHN BRUNNER, ALP., AND THE AGRICULTURAL RATING BILL.
Sir John Brunner has sent the following reply to a resolution forwarded to him by the Cheshire Chamber of Agriculture in favour of the Agricultural Land Rating Bill : _ _ _

9, Ennismore Gardens. S.W. 22nd liay, 1896. Dear Sir,—l beg to acknowledge the receipt of a copy of the resolution adopted at a general meeting of the Cheshire Chamber of Agriculture on the 18th inst.

Ragarded as a remedy for agricultural depression, the Agricultural Land Rating Bulls, in my opinion, a most cfantemptible and iaeffective production. I venture to think that agriculture suffers from no cause so much as from the fact that it is, upon the whole, the worst-man- aged business in the country. The owners of the land devote rather more attention to sport than to the industry itself, whilst the tenants, through lack of security for their capital and the work of their brains, are practically compelled to fight the whole world with one hand ticd behind their backs.— Yours faithfully,
JOHN T. BRUNNER.
Chas. B. Davies, Esq., The Secretary, The Cheshire Chamber of Agriculture.

Speakman as a County Alderman, and an election thereby rendered necessary. I have been strongly urged to allow myself to be nominated as a Candi- date for Runcorn South. To this, alter careful consideration I have consented, and trust I may so merit your confidence as to recelveyour hearty support. Within the past few years the work of the County Council has become increasingly important, and at this momentous jun;ture. wh .n it is evident that the educaticn of our children and yonth will be large'y under its control, it is im- perative that the County Council shiuld consist of those having broad, progressive, and sand Libel' :1 views, on this and many other questions which now claim the urgent attention of the Council.
I hope to have other opportunities of more fully expressing myself before the day of election. Very faithfully yours. ALFRED R. NORMAN.

In Runcorn the vacancy caused by the promotion of Mr. Speakman to the position of a county alder- man, will become the subject of a spirited contest. The notices in connection with the Runcorn South District are out, and the date for nomination of candidates is fixed for to-day (Friday) afternoon. Mr. Ashton will attend at his office on Saturday afternoon to hear and decide any objections.and the polling will take place on June tith. Mr. Norman, the candidate adopted by the Liberal Association, has issued an address,and a meeting to be addressed by Sir J. T. Brunner, Bart., is announced for Monday night. On Thursday evening a meeting of the electors of the South Division was held to con- eider the advisability or otherwise of selecting a candidate to contest the vacant seat. Mr. J. Brun- drett, J.F., occupied the chair,and there was a good [attendance. It was decided amid applause, to in- vite Mr. E,lmison to contest the division,and at the meeting Mr. Imison declared his willingness to stand. Both candidates' addresses will be found in our advertising columns.

Some interesting additions have just been made to the collection of Ashanti. relics at the Royal United Ser- vice Museum,which have attracted a very large number of sightseers during the last few days. These consist of a curious war-drum, with an elephant-hide head upon which the arummers play various rolls,al, of which have a widely differei.t significance to those who hear them. A white cloth veils the human skulls,which are fastened to either side of the instrument when tile drum is beaten on peaceful occasions. There is also a very unique; but withal primitive, urn, representing the King of Sstianti receiving a head from one of his Craurt executioners. The King is smoking a huge pipe, and being fanned at the same time by a slave girl ,whilst the band is stationed around. Both are lent by Lieutenant-Colonel Baden- Powell, who commanded the scouts in the expedition. Colonial Office collection of treasures from the Ashanti capital has also been enriched by the addition of some bead necklacesworn by King P:ascnpeh's wives, various wrist :ornaments, and other fetish charms.

The Runcorn Volunteers held their first church parade on sunday. The F and G Cona?anies of the 2nd V.R. Cheshire Regiment assembl-d at the Drill Halliand there were on parade, Captain G F. Ashton, 10 sergeants, 93 rank and file, including hand and buglers. The com- panies then marched to Holy Trinity Church, where an excellent sermon Wad delivered by the Rev. Dr. Preston. div.p: CAMP MEETING AT RUNCORN

The annual out-door services held under the direction of the Primitive Methodist Chapel took pace on Whit Sunday. In the morning a number of the congregation attended the service which was held on Runcorn Bill, where a fairly large gathering was addressed by the Rev. W. Moore, Mr. Hill, and Mr. P. Badge. In the afternoon there was a large attendance and eloquent _

_ addresses were given by Rev. T. Bramall, Mr. Spruce, Preston Brook and Mr. Peacock. SERIOUS ACCIDENT TO A RUNCORN BOY. A serious accident happened on Sunday to Robert.son of Mr. William Farrell, jun., of 12 Waterloo-road, Run- corn, who is aged ten years. The lad went home from Church and in getting over the wail at the rear of the house, a coping stone weighing about Amt. fell down upon him, fracturing his skull -very seriously. Since then the injured lad has been seen by Drs. Robinson, 11.1cLaren, and Larkin, of Liverpool, and his condition is generally regarded as hopeless. On Thurr.day the lad had not recovered consciousness.' MERSEY MISSION TO SEAMAN RUNCORN. Under the auspices of the above In.titution a capital excursion was enjoyed by about 600 people who on Whit ruesday made the journey to New Brighton from Runcorn with the specially chartered steamer—The snowdrop. A god start was made early in the morn- ing and the attractions of the Mersey watering place were thoroughly enjoyed. The return journey, with the tide was performed without mishap, Runcorn being reached shortly after ten o'clock. Mr. Shaw and the committee are to be congratulated on the completeness of their arrangements. ACCIDENT ON THE SHIP CANAL AT RUNCORN.

About roon on Monday t- he steamer Frigga after DaFs- ing under Runcorn bridge by some unaccountable reason shecrfd rieht across the waterway and cams into violent contact with the canal wall, the coping stones of which were slightly damaged. The vessel was injured about the port bow several of the plates being staved in. The injuries were all above th watermark and she was able to proceed to Manchester. div.p: DISTINGUISHED HONOUR TO A RUNCORNITE IN AUSTRALIA.

Mr. Granville-Jones, an Australian journalist, who was connected with the Chester press over a quarter of a century ago, writes to us from Queens- land the following interesting letter :—" A little over 12 months ago I had the pleasure of sending you some particulars of the success of an old Run- corn lad, Mr. IVilson Weaver Littler, and the firm of engineers (Messrs. Littler and Bruce, of the Fitzroy Foundry) of which he is the chief; and it is with great satisfaction that I now acquaint you of the fact that Mr. Littler has been elected to the die-

tinguished position of Mayor of the second city in the colony of Queensland, and what will shortly, I have no doubt, become the metropolis of the new colony of Central Queensland. Mr. Littler had completed a term of three years as alderman for the Fitzroy ward in February last, and had to seek re-election. Two opponents were brought out against him, but one retired before polling day, and the other might have followed suit, for he made but a very poor show, the old member being re- turned by a majority of two to one. Mr. Littler was proposed for the mayoralty by the retiring Mayor (Mr. Stewart Hartley), and I may say that when the result was maae known—the Council almost unanimously voting for the proposition—no one was more surprised than be. And yet Ido not see why he should have been surprised. The work he had done as an alderman showed him to be the most useful member of the Council; and as it is probable the Corporation will have to consider seriously a scheme of water eupplyfor the city during his term of office, it seemed but fit that a man possessing practical engineering knowledge should be chosen to direct its affairs at so important a juncture. At the conclusion of the election the Mayor invited the Council and a large number of friends to the Market Hotel to join him in "a social glass." Alderman Ilartley proposed "The Health of the Mayor," in a few well-chosen sentences, and the toast was responded to with musical honours and cheers for " Mr. Littler, the Mayoress, and family." Mr. Littler acknowledged the toast in an admirable little speech, in the course of which he referred to the "distressed state of the town." The distress it may be explained was due to the fact that Rock- hampton at the time the allusion was made was partly submerged by flood waters, and that a good deal of damage had been occasioned to shipping and wharves at the time. However, since then the waters have abated and the river has resumed its normal level. On the day following his election the Mayor, introduced (I think for the first time in Australia) the old custom (an annual one in Chester by the way) of " walking the marches," but in con- sequence of the flood he had to " row " instead of walk the boundaries of his dominions, a by no means pleasant task, and one not entirely unattended with danger. Alderman Hartley as- companied him, and a full and interesting account of the trip was given next day in the leading journal (the Rockhampton "Morning Bulletin.") I may add that since Mr. Littler's election to the mayoral chair he has alto been returned by virtue of his occupancy of that office to the important position ot a seat OR the first Harbour Board for the Port of Rockhampton, which was created by a special Act of Parliament passed in the last Session —a body from whicn a great_ deal is being ex- pected in the way of advancing the city and mak- ing Rockhampton the principal port of the colony. Mr. Littler's time is thus largely occupied in public business, and it speaks well for his patriotism that • he should be prepared to sacrifice so much for his adopted country. The honours and hospitalities of the position are already making their demands up- pun him in another direction, but he has been equal to them all. The other day he presided over a grand banquet given to an old Australian pioneer: the lion. Archibald Archer, of Gracemere, who has • in his time held the position of Agent-General in London and Colonial Treasurer of Queensland, but has at last retired from public life and gone .to

filngland. This week, too, Mr. Littler, accompanied by the Aldermen Bud Town Clork went to Keppel Bay and there had the honour of presenting to Lord Lamington, our new Governor, an address of wel- come to the seat of his future government. I am sure old Runcornites will be proud to learn of Mr.Littler's SUCCORS; and I can only hope it may inspire other Cheshire men, who have pluck and enterprise and intelligence, to turn their attention to this new country. It has, no doubt passed through a period of trial during the last three years, but it has come out first of all the Australian Colonies, and I believe it has entered on a splendid future.

div.head: DEATH THROUGH OVERWOTtK AT
div.p: DEATH THROUGH OVERWOTtK AT
RUNCORN.

Mr. Worsley held an inqnest at the Runcorn Police Station on the body of Joseph Faulkner, of 24 Granville- street, Rune.orn, who died on M-nday under circum- stances which necessitated an inquiry. Jane Paulkner, widow,said her husband wasp years old and had worksd at the soapworks. A week last Monday he went to work at one o'clock and came home to tea about 4.30 He afterwards went back to work until the next morning when he returned home again and had breakfast. He then went back to work and remained until dinner after which he returned again and worked until five o'clock. On getting home again he had his tea and then went te sleep. They went to bed after ten o'clock and on the Wednesday morning he ' awakened her and complained of being ill and asked her to send for a doctor. She got him a cup of tea hut he became worse and a doctor had to be called in. Dr. Robinson when he came asked her how long he had been working. She told him, and the doctor gave her some medicine and told her to poultice her hnshand which she did. He was ill all the week,and complained of a pain in his left side. ' She did not know what made him work so long, because he was not compelled to do it. Her husband told her that he had not been working all the Monday night through. He had been out of work a long time, and as they had a family of six he was anxious to get something for them. She did not know whether the manager knew that he was working so long. On the Monday night he was paid piece work but on the Tuesday he was paid by the day.—The Coroner: Would he have got into any trou- ble if he refused to work.—Witness : No Sir.—The Coroner It wag his own doing P—Witness : Yes Sir. —The Coroner: He could work as long as he liked so long as he did the job ?—Witness: Yes Sir.—The Coroner: Had he been out of work long : Witness : He had been doing three dars a week, and was very glad to pet a chance to work. John R ibinson, Greenwac-road, said he was assistant manager at the Runcorn Alkali Works. Deceased had been at the work many years and had since 1892 been fairly constantly employed. On the Monday he came to his work about noon and after working all day came back to work during the night at such times as were required. He had about one ton of slack to wheel to the fires, about every two hours. Deceased stayed on on Tuesday. He should not have stayed on by rl2hts, after working the night and day. He (witness) on the Tuesday morning asked deceased what he was doing there and told him he ought to let some one else have the work. Deceased in reply. said "It is coming Whitsuntide, let. me have it."—The Coroner: Then he worked 26 hours P—Witness ; Well you can hardly call it work wheeling a ton of coal in two hours. He could have taken 14 hours' Akan) bet ween. He could wheel about a ton in the half hour easily, and would have nothing to do until the end of the two hours. It was not usual for men to work that length of time and he would not have allowed deceased to do so if he had not rsk Id to stop On.—The Coroner : I suppose he wanted to earn the extra money P—Witness : Yes,for Whitsuntide. I would not have let him do it only the man had been on short work.—The Coroner: There was no compulsion on the part of the company ?—Witness: Nia ; there was none whatever.

Dr. Robinson sail he was called in on the Wednesday morning ani saw the deceased repeatedly until Monday innrning. He found him in a complete state of collapsil, rambling and talking about toetball. A slight reaction set in but pneumonia supervened from which he died on the following Alon..lay morning.—The Coroner : You questioned him. Ivitness : On, yes; because it was the third ease of a similar nature I have had during the last fortnight. Two recovered. They , were not from the same works.—The Coroner : How do you mean Witness: From over exertion.—The Coroner : From working long hours? Witness : Yes, work- ing at heavy work for long hours.—The Coroner: To what would you attribute death P—Wit- ness : To coneestion of the lungs trnught on by over exertion.—The Coroner : Then you attribute congestion of the lungs to over exertion P—Witness : Distinctly— Coroner: Was he able to tell you anything P—Witness Oh, perfectly. At first he rambled but was able to talk when the reaction set in :—The Coroner: Was it his own doing ?—Witness as far as I knew, there was no com- pulsion. The man was very glad to have the extra work. —The Coroner : There is no supposition in the case that deceased was in any way compelled.—Witness ; I did not understand that at all—The Coroner : If anything there was, contention to get the work. Witness : I have heard so. This was the whole of the evidence offered. The Coroner in putting the case to the jury, said he could not think there was any blame attached to the works He thought the man had undertaken the work himself and there had been no compulsion put upon him. If there had been compulsion—if the man had been compelled or pressure pet upon him to do the work— there would have been a different story to tell. After a short consultation the jury returned a verdict of " death by pneumonia, brought on by over exertion"
WHIT-MONDAY AT RUNCORN.

div.head: ANNUAL PROCESSIONS.
div.p: THE ANNUAL PROCESSIONS.

Whit-Monday, the most important and enjoyable holi- day of the year to Runcorn people, opened with ideal weather which continuing through the day ensured the successful termination to the day's proceedings. In the morning many visitors began to pour into the streets of Runcorn, and early in the day the thoroughfares be- gan to assume an unwonted appearance of life and gaiety. Most of the business houses in the town were closed, and the streets with a large display of bunting were appropriate, and at the same time by their appear- ance pointed to a general holiday. In the morning there was the usual

PARADE OF FRIENDLY SOCIETIES but unfortunately much of the dignity and the pleasure from a sight-seeing, point of view was lost by the fact that the three societies which did turn out, acted independently and chose their own route and time of starting making three poor processions, which badly filled the place of one well organised turn out. The members of the Dul.:e's Club met in front of Bridgewater House on the green, and from that spot proceeded through Duke's Fuld-, into Church-st.,and then through Greenw ay-road, Eligh•st., and Halton-road, OS far as the Crane, and afterwards returned to Devon- shire Square. Several of the members appeared in their regalia and amongst the 80 members taking part were:— Dr. Robinson, Dr. McKenzie, Messrs. Meadowcroft, Rawlinsen, Fullan, I'. Sinsister, T. Done (treasurer), W. Hoxworth (secretary), G. S. Hollingworth, W. lox- worth, J. Pencilebury, W. Johnson, W. Miller, J. Miller, J. Jones, R. FazAckerley, Joseph Flarrop, Thomas Harri- son, H. Crompton and Joseph Rose (committee). The procession was headed by the banner of the order and closely followed by the members of the Volunteer band.

The members of the Rote of Sharon Lodge of thel Grand United Order of Oddfeliows mustered about nine o'clock at the lodge-room. A good number of the mem- bers turned up and headed by the banner, representing on one of its sides the Arms of the Lodge and on the other allegorical pictures representing the relief of sick- ness and distress,and the Widnes subscription band, the members paraded the chief streets of the town to Lea- lane and retired by Union-street, Victoria-road, Green- way-road, Byrom-street and Shaw-street to the lodge room. The regalia of the members was very striking and added to the picturesque effect of the procession. Amongst those with the procession were :—Dr. McLennan. Dr. Hutchinson, Dr. Robinson, and the offiers, T. L. Ashcroft, warden ; Bro. Moston, of Star of Freedom Lodge, Bros. J. Douglas (treasurer), W. Massey (stTretary).E. Jones, G. Rutter and W. Lambert (trustees). S. Moulselale, PG., James Ashley, N.G., F. Scrutton, V.G., S. Cliff and J. Rogerson (guardians). Following this lodge was the Juvenile Society,headed by the Nelson-street Drum and Fife Band, some of the vounger members being driven in the procession in a float sent by Mr. Scott. A fairly large gathering of the Watermen and Porters' Association assembled at the Brunner Guild Hall. The procession was headed by the Aston and Preston Brook Band, who gave a very good selection of music en route. Amongst those in the procession were Mr. Billiam, pre- sident; Mr. Banner, vice-president; Mr. Caldwell, trea- surer; and Mr. Gatley, secretary, The members num- bered about 100, and banners and samples of the craft carried by several added to the general effect of the turn out. The route selected and traversed by this club lay along High-3r., Church-st., Egertor-st., Greenway- road, Victoria-road, over Delph Bridge and from that point back to the Lodge room. In the afternoon mem- bers and friends alike sat town to tea, which was followed by a pleasant entertainment and dance.

div.head: CHURCH SCHOOLS.
div.p: THE CHURCH SCHOOLS.

The scholars of the schools incorporated with the Church of England in the district a-,sembled at their heal quarters shortly after noon. At one o'clock the different soh -ols naving meta, long procesa!on moved off through Church-street,Bridge-street,Victoria-roat4 to the field opposite the vicaray,e. The procession was headed by the Runcorn Volunteer band and after the banner was the Parish Church school with which were the Revs.

H. B. Firth. and W Sell°les ; Messrs. John Littler (super- intendant), James Littler, Henry Branch, James Moores, J. Johnson, J. Yates, J. Wilson, F. Rutter, F. Wilkinson, J. Hewitt, R. Abel, J. E. Langshaw, W. E. Dudley, Clare, Crowther, W. Rolch, Ahley. Catrow, and Hulse. The number of scholars was set down at 600 females and 450 males and as the children were gaily dressed and banners and other emblems occurred at frequent inter- vals in the line of the procession, a very pleasing effect was produced. Behind the Parish Church schools were the Holy Trinity, Mill Brew Ragged and Mariners' Church schools, led by the Mill Brow fife and drum hand. Amongst those prominent in connection with the schocls were—Wvs. Dr. Preston and A. H. Bertram, Messrs. Westbrook, Broughton, Kilcross, Turner, Bazley, J. Woods, Wilkinson, Sweetman, and Bate, the Misses Preston, Marsh, E. Turner. and Horsefield. The total number of scholars consisted of about 300.
The Meraey Mission to Seamen followed with about 220

children Who were led by the Widnes Subscription band. With this body were Messrs. Shaw (missionary),J.Rose, W. Byheld, Kelly, G. Kenwright, W. Marsh, Joseph Evans, F. Hirst, and J. Price. A number of the _ _

children were dressed in seamen's costume and looked very neat. The rear of the procession was brought up by the children of St. Michaels school; number- ing about 290 scholars. and 21 teachers. In their ranks were the Rev. FL C. Moyle, Messrs Sherlock, Austin, Cropper, C. Povvnall, W. Cooke and J. H. Austin, (secre- tary). The! children with the exception of the scholars lelon2in2 to Fink Trinity and its branches, spent the evening in a field off Greenway-road, tea being served at the different schoolrooms. The Holy Trinity scholars took possession of a field placed at the disposal of the Committre by Mr. Hulse, and an enjoyable evening was spent. At St. Michaels an interesting miscellaneous con- cert was given, and the programme was thoroughly en- joyed.

div.head: NON-CONFORMIST SCHOOLS
div.p: THE NON-CONFORMIST SCHOOLS

held their annual field day on the Common to where they marched in processional order along Church-street, Regent-ltreet, and Greenway-road. The procession was of course headed by the oldest school (Brunswick-street Wesl, yan Schools), who were preceded by their banner. In the procession were en route, Messre. J. Simpson, T. Simister, R. Rawlinson, E. Taylor, A. R. Norman, B. Knivston, and G. Millington. The number of scholars belonging to this institution who took rart was 5,500. St. John's Presbyteidan Sunday School, followed rioht of priority with scholars numbering 218 After the banner came Messrs. J. Pritchard, R. W. Herron, J E. Warburton (superintendents), James Kirkham )Itiavl), Thomas Dobson, Gatley (secretaries), Fe Williams, J. Steele, John Pritchard, Jepson, Baxter, Hou,hton, Hewitt an; Wilkinson. St. Lukes' School followed next, headed by Messrs. J. J. Speakman (vice president). J. Slade, T. Worrall (superintendents). P. Cartwright (secretar), Wood, G. Lacy, S. Mousdale. S. Booth. It. Lewe, J. Gayter, and G. Clark, with 121 scholar and teachers, and then csme Bethesda Congre- gatienal School with 193 members, led by the Rev. J. S. Simpson, Messrs. Taylor (superintendent), F. Cring- hall (secretary). C. C. le Couteur (treasurer). H. Chad- wick, Walton, Cringhall, Davies, Ackerlev, Fleathering- con and Lunt. The St. Edward's Catholic School who were headed by their own brass band included the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. Donc.y, J. P. Quinn, Nickson, J. Dowd, J. P. Wheelan, and Williamson, and amongst this hocly'which numbered 332 were the members of the League of the Cress and the Society of the Children of Mary. The next school was the Primitive Methodist Sunday school, Greenwa.y-road, numbering about 348 scholars and amongst those in attendance were the Revs' G. Bramsll and W. Moore ; Messrs. Sayle, Hillidge, Richardson (superintendents), John Fleet .(secretary), E. Aston (treasurer), Goodier (Crewe),Postles (Chester), Hayes, Reynolds, Royle, and Peacock. In advance of Mill Brow school wnich came next with 300 scholars were—Rev. W. George, Messrs. S. Pope, r. Findlow (superintendents), G. W. Yates (secretary), E. Moorfield (tressurer),C. Lloyd (superintendent of infants), Comes, Sweetman, Reylloce, Haddock, lace, (Lostock), and W. Yates. The Ellesmere United Methodist Free Church paraded 216 persons, amongst whom were the Rev. J. Stafferd, Messrs. Gandy, F. Clarke (superintendents), J. Helford (secretary), G. White (treasurer), Newall, G. Paul, T. Parry, Seragg, E. Jones, M. Tern- perler, W. Fowles, F. Guy, John Curzon, Jannion, T. Clarke, P. Shaw, H. Nield, and T. Moores. Behind them came the scholars of the Camden School, with an imposing array of 495 scholars lead by Messrs. P. Soeakman, J.P., C. Aid, A. Harrison (superintend- ants), S. Littler, J. Naslor (secretaries), J. Dutton (trea- surer), G-orge Littler. T. Rwe, Nilkinson.J. B. Clarke, S. Baeey, W. Tickle, J. Willis ms,J. Shaw, C. Ditchfield, J. Rowe and J. Dean, and they were followed by Nelson- street with a body of 130 scholars and teachers, the offieers being Messrs. Littlemore, Lambert, Malinger, Hughes and Soutley. The rear of the procession was brought up by the scholars from the Gospel Mission, Hope Hall, with their superintendent, Mr. J. Lightfoot. Tea was provided for the scholars by the respective school committees and afterwards the Common was the scene of a two hours' outdoor revelry. The scholars attending the Mill Brow sch ola occupied a field lent by Mr. Sweetman and visited Rvdal Mount, the resiJence of Mr. S. Taylor, J P., C.C., where fruit and light refreshments were distributed.
ATTRACTIONS IN THE TOWN.

Very little berond the procession was provided for the attraction of visitors. As usual the fair ground was the scene of a pleasure fair comprising aunt-sallies, merry- gr—rounds, lollipop stalls, and cheat) shows, which all received a fair amount of patronage daring the after- noon and evening. __ _

div.head: HALTON.
div.p: HALTON.

HALTON WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCITOOL.—The usual treat was helo on Whit-Monday afternoon. The weather was beautifully fine, and there was a big gathering. The number of persons in the procession was 350, and as they walked round the village with flags and banners flying, they made a very pleasing sight. Some of the e.chol4rs were prevented by sickness from being present, and as the precession passed their homes a halt was made whilst a hymn was sung. Mr. W. Nixon kindly lent" Duke's "field for the occasion, and there various kinds of recreation were heartily engaged in. A pleasant feature of these treats is the presencs of former scholars who now reside elaewhere ; and this year the number

was unusually large. Many of the parents also came into the field, and greatly enj,,yed themselves. Tea was provided at 4.15, in the schoolroom. The following ladies presided at the tables : Mesdames Bedrick,.Millechamp, _

dare, S. Hughes, J. T. Hughes, M. Dunbabin, Mowbray Higginson, S. Ravrlinson, Cox, and pruce. After tea the games in the field were resumed, races run, and a quantity of nuts scattered. At 830, the company stood at the front of the chapel, and sang a hymn and the doxology. Three hearty cheers were given for Rev. C• de P. Gliddon, Messrs. H. Rowe (superintendent) W. and J. Nixon, and D. Barrow, also for the workers of the Sunday school,and those who in anyway helped to make the day a succes.

div.head: WESTON.
div.p: WESTON.

At Weston this year's Church demonstration was if anything a greater success than that of any previous year. The scholars and friends numbered about 600, so that it was not only one of the largest processions which has ever passed through the village, but was noticeable for great taste and decoration. Next followed the school brass band of 25 perfermers, and then the Women's Bible Class and female scholars. A lorry containing the small girls separated this banner from the choir boys, 20 in number, who followed in Eton dress, each young gentleman with his carefully-selected buttonhole fib rer. The choir boys were headed by their own banner, borne by G. Molyneaux, dressed as a Burgher's Chanter of the 14th century. Next came the superb Men's Bible Class banner, which first saw the light on Sunday last. Two lurries with little boys brought up the rear. The Weston churchpeople are to be congratulated on their grand dis- play, as well as on the great progress the school has evi- dently made in the village during the past year. The annual demonstration of the Wesleyan Suuday School was held en Whit-Monday. The day was beau- tifully fine. Soon after one o'clock the scholars com- menced to assemble at the school, from which the pro- cession was arranged to start. At the time fixed the Weston Band (which is coneected with the school),under the conductorship of M. John Smith, took its place at the head of the procession, end a start was made to- wards Runcorn, along the Weston-road, the route fol- lowed in previous years heing also followed this year. The scholars were marshalled by the superintendents and teachers of the school, Mr. James Ball being in charge. Excellent order was kept, as the teachers took charge of their own classes. The banner, which shows the school was founded in the year 1832, was carried by two of the elder scholars. The final stand was made, as usual, round the" Cross," after which the scholars were entertained to tea at the school. Great praise is tine to Mr. William Dunbabin for the excellent manner in which he had his lorry de- corated. The waggon was filled with little children and several old residents. Subeequent to the children's tea the senior scholars and members of the congregation sat down ta tables pis sided over by Mesdames Price, Griffiths, Kirkham, Smith and Spruce, Misses Danbabin and S svage. After tea the scholars had the use of a field kindly lent for the occasion, and engaged in games till darkness set in. The committee of the school are entitled to great praise for the success of this year's "children's day," and that their efforts are appreciated is shown by the fact of so many oil scholars and mem- bers of the congregation joining in the festivi ies. The number this year was 330, whish is largely in excess of previous years.

div.head: FRIENDLY SOCIETY MEETINGS.
div.p: FRIENDLY SOCIETY MEETINGS.
MANCTIESTEB UNI TY.

The A.M.C. of the Manchester Unity of OddfellowS opened on Monday at Bristol. The Grand Master in his inaugural address pointed cut that 1.000 new members were enrolled per m -,ntb, and that the capital now stood at nine millions sterling. The Order, he said, was in the grand position of being the largest and wealthist adult benefit society in the world. In regard to old-age pen- sions, he advised that provision for old age sheuld b. made one of the ordinary benefits of friendly societies, and that self-help should be relied upon by working men instead of State subsidies. Mr. Strachey's Old-age Pen- sion Bill he thrught the delegates would condemn unani- mously. A discussion arose afterw +rd., in reference to the action of the Liverpool police in in!ruding upon lodge meetings in public-houses—a practice which was consid- ered highly objectionable. The matter was referred to the Friendly Societies Conference.

_ ... . The A.M.C. of the Manchester Unity of 0 ldfellows was continued on Tuesday at Bristol. The Parliamen- tary Agent stated that the Government had prepared a useful bill consolidating the Acts relating to friendly societies, and he suggested that they should be asked to introduce it and press it forward. A report was made. that some of the lodges were in the habit of paying for drink in the guise of rent. The practice was described as illegal, and was strongly condemned. The directors reccmmended that advantage he takon of the new Friendly Societies Act by admitting members from the age of one year. This was agreed tn. la discussion also took place upon a propnaal to so alter the rules that the Order would take full receonsiuility for the female lodges. Brother Graham, in this cnnneetion, expressed great dissatisfaction with the decision of the Northamp- ton A.M.C. in his year of offine as Grand Master. By a large majority, it was decided to eliminate the clause objected to. The Manchester Unity of Odd fellows at the meeting in Bristol on Wednesday discussed the clear- ance question. A Portsmouth delegate proposed a reso- lution to facilitate the transfer of members who had re- moved, hut it was bjected to this that it would throw the whole constitution of the Unity into the melting-pot, as it would lead young men to desert the lodges which were not financially sound in order to join those which were better situated. The motion was lost. A Ton- bridge delegate proposed the establishment of a fund to provide for the boarding-out of the orphans of deceased members. A koßlackburn delegate pointed out that.- they had not yet provided for their old members; and the motion was lost. Complaint was made that certain printing work was being done at less than trade union prices,but the discussion of the matter came to a premature end by the adoption of the closure —an incident which occasioned some excitement.

At Thursday's meeting of the Manchester Unity of Oddfeliows a discussion took place up,n the'," strained relations" between the medical pinfession and the medical associations in various parts of the coutitry. Complaint was made that medical men endeavoured 0 prevent members of the profession from acting as medical officers to these associations, and, more than this, that they had sought to restrict the membership of friendly societies to men earning only 2bs. or 30s. per week. On the other hand, it was contended that medical men had just as much right to combine in their own interests as working men had to join trade unions. Upon a division a motion asking for Parliamentary assistance in the matter was lost by 235 votes to 195. A. proposal that superannuation and sick benefits should run concurrently was rejected.

div.head: AHEPHERDS.
div.p: THE AHEPHERDS.

• The Loyal Order of Ancient Shepherds opened ita annual meeting on Monday at Newcastle-on-Tyne. The Chief Shepherd ,Brother G. Evans.of Nantwich,discussed the financial position,and urged the impnrtance of taking to heart the lesslns • aught by the valuati-Ins. Referring to old-age pensions,he said it was'well-known that there was no great desire for them among the members of friendly societies.and he was afraid that would continue so long as they received a pension in the form of con- tinous sick pay. This was a benefit for which no pro- vision was made.and he suggested that at a given age sick pay should cease and a pension take its place. In the discussion which followed a Shea3ld delegate urged that all new entrants should be compelled to pay to an old-age pension fund.

div.head: EVERY PERSON'S FUTURE.
div.p: EVERY PERSON'S FUTURE.

Every person's future is, to a certain 'extent,. in hi own hand. Many a future which might have been bril- liant has been darkened by lack of the spirit of self-help. Many a home might have been gladdened by life and health and comfort, has been saddened by poverty, illness and death, in many cases wholly preventible. The spring and summer months are, from a sanitary point of view, among the most important of the year. Due care may now mean a healthy and happy sammer and autumn, and robust constitution to meet the trials of next winter. Neglect may now mean a joyless sum- mer, a trying autumn, and a broken constitution to succumb under the attacks of any exceptional trial. There are indeed few that do not feel the system needs recruiting. With some it is " only a little cough," "tendency to bronchitis," and others," not quite up t the mark," "a sort of all over sinking feeling," " too weak to do anything about the house," "these recurring headaches,"" no appetite for his food," Sze. These and a dozen others are common expressions which all point to the urgent need of some good tonic. What change of air can do for you in a few months' time—if you are no worse then than you are now—a course of some good tonic mixture, a reliable medicine of established reputa- tion and of proved virtue will do now. • There are several tonic mixtures to be had, but none which have been so uniformly successful as Gwilym Evans' Quinine Bitters, the Vegetable Tonic.'

SLEEPING OUT.—Selina Giblin and John Sharky, !a dock labourer, was charged with sleeping out in a house in Water- at.. at 4 a.m. on Tuesday morning.—P.C. .Wylie stated the case and both prisoners pleaded guilty. The male prisoner was fined 10s. and costs or 14 days, and Giblin was sent to gaol for 14 days without the option of a fine. THE THREE CARD TRlCE.—Lewis Illingworth, of North- wich, answered to a clot:ge of gaming by means of a three card trick on the Fairground. Runcorn, on Saturday.—k.C. Gregory stated that he was on duty on the Fairground about 10 p.m., and saw a crowd round the prisoner, who was play- ing the three card trick. He saw money passed, and a man in the crowd lost 2s. Prisoner who said he had a wife and four children was sent to gaol for 7 days.

div.head: WARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.

A meeting of this Council was held in the Bewsey Chambers Warrington, on Wednesday afternoon. Mr. W. Houghton occupied the chair, and there were also present Messrs. J. Houghton, G. Thompson, T. Halton, J. Johnson, J. Warburton, J. W. Knowles, J. Ball,-S. Sutton (clerk), F. Kerfoot (nuisance inspector).

div.head: RE-APPOINTMENT OF OFFICERS, –
div.p: RE-APPOINTMENT OF OFFICERS, -

The CHAIBMAN moved the re-appointment of Dr. Seph- ton as medical officer-at a salary-of £lOO per annuna,and also the re-appointment of Mr. F. Kerfoot as nuisance inspector at a yearly salary of £llo.—Mr. Halton se- conded, and the motion was unanimously agreed to.

div.head: TUE PAYMENT, FOR THE NOTIFICATION OF DISEASES
div.p: TUE PAYMENT, FOR THE NOTIFICATION OF DISEASES

A communication was read from the Hates Owen (Worcestershire) Rural Council, asking the Council to petition in favour of the fee for the notification of in- fectious diseases by medical practitioners being fixed at the uniform rate of one shilling—The Chairman said. it was only a few years since that the Council decided to pay for the notification of infectious diseases. They had previously had it done without payment, but they now paid 2s. 61 each case.—The Clerk pointed oUr that the sum paid amounted to about £6 or £8 per annum.—Mr. Knowles said so long as the sum was so small it was not necessary to bother in altering the attount.—Mr. Thompson mcved, and Mr. Ball seconded, that the com- munication lie on the table.—This was agreed to.

div.head: DANGEROUS FOOTPATII.
div.p: A DANGEROUS FOOTPATII.

The CLERK read a letter from Mr. John E. Richard- sun, of Paddington House, 'Paddington, in which atten- tion was called to the present dan,,erous and unsatis- factory state of the footpath off Manchester-road be- tween the stile leading to Paddington Station and the entrance to Paddington proper.—The Clerk said he had written to Mr Richardson asking him to direct the at- tention of the Highway Board to the matter. SURVEYOR'S REPORT.—WINWICS DRAINAGE.

The SURVEYOR reported that during the month inspec- tions had been made of Mr. Ezard's house and Mr. Hindley's at Padgate and new sheds at Sankey Wire Mills. A certificate of habitation had been issued to Mr. William Htndley for two houses at Padgate. The following plans were submitted for approval :—New hay barn arra shippon at Causeway Bridges Farm;Burton- wood. for Lord Lilford ; Messrs. Greenall Whitley and Company' newoutbuildings at the Chapel House Inn, Great Sankev. Referring to the Winwick drainage, in respect of which he had been directed to undertake plans levels, and specifications, he reported that as portions of the drain belonging to the County Council wcre proposed to be used by the Rural Council the firAt step was to get the necessary permission from the County Council. He (Mr. Owen had had an interview wail Mr.Thompson,the surveyor to the District Highway Board, from whom he obtained the exact position of the existing lengths. Per- miision had since been granted by the County Council provided the Rural Council took over the existing lengths of drain and ever afterwards maintained and re- paired them and permitted the highway drains to enter them at any point and at any time considered desirable. Providing no legal objections arose, the whole of the work would have to be done to the satisfaction of the Highway Board.—The Clerk said there were no legal objzBtions ; the only point was.whether the Council .was prepared to take over the drains and maintain them for pet petuit:i.—:lt was decided on the proposition of Mr. Knowle3, seconded b 7 Mr. Ball, that the suggestions of Mr. Owen, be carried out.

div.head: PADGATE DRAINAGE
div.p: PADGATE DRAINAGE

The SURVEYOR further reported that at a meeting of the Streets Committee it WAS decided to recommedd the District Council to sewer the district by connecting with the sewers of the Corporation of Warrington providing satisfactory terms could be made with the Corporation for the reception. of the sewage into their .system of sewers. It was also decided to recommend tho District Council not to proceed for the present with the sewer so. far as the length , from Bruche Bridge to Paddington Cottages was cencerned, providie,g some arrangement could be made for dealing with the sewage of the cot- tages in Soapery Row close to Spittle Bridge. The clerk and surveyor were instructed to have a preliminary in- terview with the ToWn Clerk and the Borough Surveyor so that if possible they might be in a position to report something with regard to terms at the meeting of the District Council .on the 7ch. The Town Clerk and Borough Surveyor were agreed that subject to the ap- proval of the Town Council, the negotiations for payment for enteiing and using the Corporation sewers should be on the following basis : each house or other building connected witll the sewer and empty- ing itself into the new sewer should pay a certain sum in the £ pm. annum calculated on its rateable value; that the amount be collected by the overeeers of the t-iwnship and be paid over to the Corporation. Before the Town Clerk acid the Borough Surveyor woulabe ready to negiotate the amount in the £ to be paid the Borough Surveyor would have to inspeet the district and a calculation would have to be made as to the probable rateable value. From als inspvtion made of Soapery Row it would appear that there would be no difficulty in draining it so as not to he a nuisance to the brook On the motion of Mr. Flatten, seconded by M:. Knowles, Mr. Owen's scheme was adopted. This concluded the business.

div.head: WHAT GIVES WAY FIRST.
div.p: WHAT GIVES WAY FIRST.

We all know that the strength of a chain is only equa to the strength of its weakest link. We often use this fact to illustrate our arguments. If a person has in- herited or acquired any constitutional weakness, we say that his t trength is determined by this weakness, That is, if for any reason there is a strain on his system, the weak point will give way first. A man who has a weak stomach suffers in his stomach for all his indiscretions. Here is the Case of a gentleman whose stomach gave way under the strain of influenzi, : 0 " Some three or four years ago I had a severe attack of irtfilltACZA. leaving behind it as a legacy a recurrence, often from day to day, of mast excruciating spasms in the region of my stomach, frequently after meals. Iso suffered for three years, trying every remedy under the sun, but all proved of no avail. lat last bethoughb me that I would try Scott's Emulsion, which at that time a very delicate girl was taking to her great benefit. After taking, say half-a-dczen bottles or so, I seemed to gain more strength and put more flesh on to my bones, which before were appreciably getting more exposed. The pain seemed to gradually lessen as I gained flesh and strength, my food reamed to digest better, and the pains became only of two or three months' recurrence. Per- sisting still in taking Scott's Emulsion up to the presen date, I may say that I am now perfectly cured of these pains, and am well and healthy in every respect. verily believe, had I not taken in hand your valuable fonic,l should not now have been alive to bear testimony to the valuable properties of Scott's Emulsion, which I am now constantly recommending (arid with marvel- lous effect in many Cases) to all suffering similarly as I have for years suffered. My friends can all bear testi- mony to tne wonderful changes it has effected on my constitution, and with every feeling of gratitude to you, I beg to subscribe myself, yours faithfully, (signed), F. S. COLQUEIOUN. The [fall, Owston Ferry, Bawtry, January 20.:h, 1896." _

The -explanation of Mr. Colguhoun's case is that Scott's Emulsion gave him strength to overcome the weakness in his stomach 'without taxing the stomach. He was evidently deriving no nourishment from his food. This reduced him to emaciation, and naturally aggrav- ated his stomach difficulty. Scott's Emulsion is nour- ishment partially digested. This was just what his weakened system needed to gain strength ,and thus over- c ;me the difficulty in his stomach. •

div.head: CITOOL BOARD ELECTION AT DARESBURY.
div.p: CITOOL BOARD ELECTION AT DARESBURY.

The triennial election of a School Board for the united parishes of Daresbury, Newton-by-Dares- bury, Hatton, Preston Brook, Keckwick, Acton Grange, Moore, and Higher Walton, ha v taken place, without a poll being demanded. At the time appointed, Mr. Aiiiton, reurning officer, received the following twelve nominations for the seven seats :—Alfred Broome, Crow Nest Farm, Keck- wick, farmer; Thomas S. Burgess, ktoWs tlropcl Farm, estate agent; Rev. H. T. Clark, future vicar of Daresbnry ; John Cooper, Higher Walton, corn merchant; Miss Bessie Dutton, The Willows, Moore ; Peter Gleave, Moore, provision dealer ; Henry Mawdsley, Hatton, farmer: C. W. Phillips, Ring O'Bells, Daresbury ; George Rodger. Newton-by-Darekbury, merchant; Charles Roy- lance, Moore, farmer; Peter Tickle, Preston Brook, farmer: John White, Moore Hall, estate agent. A meeting of eight of the above, with their proposers and seconders, was held in the Sessions room, on Saturday morning, at 9.30, for the purpose of en- deavouring to arrange matters in order to avoid a poll, the Rev. J. Gilbertson presiding. Nothing de- finite conici be settled at that meeting, but laterin the afternoon an arrangement was made which leaves the following elected members of the Board : —Rev. H. T. Clark, vicar of Daresbury ; Captain Rodger. Newton Bank,Newton-by-Dareshury ' • Miss B. Dutton, Monrk; Mr. Alfred Broome. K,Tkwick; Peter Tickle, Preston Brook ; C. W. Phillips, Dares- bury; John Cooper, Higher Walton. The first three mentioned persons are new members of the Board, the last four were members of the old Board.

One of till; peasl- ants died after seven years' imprisonment,the other will be liberated.

div.head: NOTES AND NEWS.
div.p: NOTES AND NEWS.

The Midland Railway Company have accepted tenders for the supply of Barnsley hard steam ceal for the ensu- ing year at the same price as last year, 7s. pr ton. The fact is of impoitanee to the trade of Sout. Yorkshire as a whole, inasmuch as the rates for this class of fuel have a very considerable influence on .contract figures gener- ally. Owing to the probable ending of the Conciliation Board and the existing agreement with the Miners' Fed- eration in August next, and the fact that the Durham miners have given notice to tenni:tate their Conciliation Board agreement, colliery owners had found some difficulty in agreeing to terms of tender, but 7s. was fixed upon and, so far as hest qualities are concerned, has been accepted without demur. The price is the same aswas agreed to by the North-E istern Railway Company in December last, when an attempt to obtain an addi- tional 6th per ton failed, and Mr. B. Pickard, m.r., reminded tha colliery owners that no reduction of wages would be accepted merely because of failure to maintain an agreed contract price. The Lancashire and York- shire Company a year ago contracted for supplies at 6s. 9d. per ton, but has not yet placed its South York- shire contracts for the ensuing year.

In Switzerland from the smallest village it is now possible (according to a consular report) to telephone to any place in the country at a fee of from one penny to fourpence for the most diAant points, on instruments on which one can hear with perfect distinctness, and which are kept in thorough repoir. The Oectric light is flaw installed in every modarafe-lized village,the motive power being„water.

A plague of caterpillars is one of the troubles of the dry season, especially in Surrey. Many trees are prac- tically divested of their foliage by these lame. The oak trees, in particular, on the road irom Leith Hill to Holm- wood present a remarkable appearance. From the now almost leafless branches of many of them hang thiek curtains of caterpillar threads on which the grubs are descending one after another to the ground in order to make their way to some fresh pasturage. The numbers are remarkable, and evoke incessant exclamations from the pedestrians. These are not always exclamations of wonder. It is a decided drawback to the pleasures of a country walk to find yourself suddenly breaking a miniatura forest of thin-spun viscrius threads, wnich bring down upon you a shower of creeping things. It is to be hoped that a deluge of rain will soon free the country of this plague, which is doubtless playing havoc with the orchard trees as well as with the Surrey -oaks.

Dr. Parker, in the course of his sermon on Sunday evening, took occasion to characterise the bicycle as 4* that shoulder-contracting, mlschievoui, hprrible machine that will take the manliness out of any nation."

An American grievance against England, which cer- tainly cannot be dealt with by any diplomatic means, is the increased multiplication of the English sparrow. On this side of the water he is noisy and impudent, but un- der "the stars and bars "he has:developed into a veri- table ruffian. A recent issue of the Chicago "Sunday Tribute has a series of illustrations devoted to por- traying the enornaLies of the imported " tyrant of Lin- coln ?ark," while the acmmp.inying letter-press des- cribes bow the " fcatliered bully " attacks every free- born American bird. The sparrows worry to death snow birds, blackbirds, robins, the Parula warbler, and even • make the life of the "lanky American bittern" a bur- den to him.

Regulations have been prepared for the trials of self- moving vehicles competing for the twe prizes of £lOO each alai two of £5O each respectively, for light and heavy loads, to be offered at the Manchester meeting of the Royal AgrieWtural Society next year. The light load class will be for such self-moving vehicles as would take the place of the light spring cart, for the convey- ance of loads up to two tons exclusive of the weight of the vehicles. The heavy load class will be for vehicles capable of taking five tons. In both cases the vehicles are to be propelled exclusively by mechanical mean. The trials will be over not less than 50 miles out and 50 miles return, during which run the consumption of fuel and water will be carefully noted. The maximum speed is to be at the rate of ten miles an hour. The points to which the special attention of the judges are to be called are due regard to the convenience of the public, ease of handling with special reference to stopping,starting,and steering, strength of design, and weight of vehicle.

The city of Montpelier, in France, is said to be the first to regulate the kind of wrapping paper that articles of food shall be delivered in. Coloured paper is abso- lutely forbidden. Printed paper and old manuscripts may only be used for dried vegetables. For all other articles of food new paper, either white or straw- coloured, must be used.

Some figures published by a French scientist may possibly in some measure tend to resl rict the indiscrim- inate teaching of music to very young children. It is declared that a large number of nervous maladies from which girls of the present day suffer are to be attributed to playing the piano. Children who ought to be exer- cising in the open air are kept at dreary and distasteful work at the keyboard hour after hour daily, and the nerves simply will not stand the strain. It is said to be proved by statistics that of 1,000 girls who study this instrument before the age of 12, no less than 600 suffer from this class of disorders, while of those who do not begin until later there are only some 200 per 1,000. The proportion among those who are spared the practice is only 100 per 1,000. The remedy suggested is that chil- dren should not be permitted to study music before the age of 16.

"4 Oom Paul" is to be" executed in bronze" while yet he lives, for the admiration and encouragement of the hardy Boers over whose destines he presides with such consummate skill. During the reioicings over the opening of the Delagoa Bay Railway to the Transvaal, when there was a great gathering of South African governors and notables at Pretoria, and sentiments of the most friendly character were exchanged, Mr. S. Narks (of Lewis and Marks), who has made a fortune in the Republic and ,a an ardent admirer of President Kruger, made an offer to erect to him a statue at a cost of £lO,OOO. The offer was accepted, but the Jameson raid and the clash of arms have interfered with its ful- filment. However, the Cape mail now brings the news that Mr. A. Van Wouw has prepared a deign which has been accepted. A base of granite will support a column of marble or granite, and upon this will stand a bronze statue of the President in his habit as he lives, frock coat and tall hat included. The monument will be a total height of 40ft. and on the corners will be re- presented four of" Oom Paul's faithful burghers.

Dr. Samuel Smiles, the famous author of" Self-Help," is rapidly recovering from the injury caused by his recent severe fall. The doctor is eights-four, and it is lac wonder that there was a general fear of the mishap proving serious. Dr. Smiles can look back on a singularly active and fruitful career. He was born in Haddington. and for some years practised as a surgeon, but aban- doned the art for journalism, becoming the editor of the " Leeds Times." He v as afterwa;rds secretary of a Leeds Railway Company, and tor the twelve years ending in 1866 he was connected with the South-Eastern. That year he retired. His works are voluminous. The faniqus " Self-Help " appeared thirty-seven years ago, but he had already published a " Life of George Stephenson," a "History of Ireland," and matter on the diverse topics af railway property and physical education. His later writing has been very extensive, ranging over history, "biography, ethics, invention, and industry. Lie is a " Quarterly Reviewer."

Difficulties have risen 'with regard to the administra- tion of Baron Hitch's estate. Mor- than oqe of the exe- cutors named by the testator have refused to act, and complications have also arisen from the manner in which the will is drawn. It is expected that the property in England which will pay duty to the Chancellor of the Exchequer will fall little short of £3,000,000. .

Dean Farrar has had the satisfaction of seeing yet another edition of his" Life of Christ." It has juht been issued by Messrs. Cassell. The Dean is now sixty-five. It is a far cry to his early days in Bombay, where his father was a missiomary. England he first saw when quite a child, and he was sent to school for some time to the Isle of Man, subsequently to King's College, Lon- don. He soon gave earnest of the ability that was in him. Greater proof was forthcoding in his Cambridge days. His first hook was a study of school-life. Philo- logy and metaphysics fascinated him for many a year. While Head Master of Malborough College, he wrote 4‘ The Life of Christ," far and away the most popular of his books, whatever its shortcomings. His clerical and controversial career is a long story, but a familiar one

In Wednesday's sitting of the Chamber of Representa- tives M. Cartayvels called the attention of the House to the importation into Belgium of old horses from Eng- land, which were afterwards killed and converted into tinned meat. No fewer than 6,000 horses had, lie said, thus entered Belgium in the course of last year. The pea ker pointed out that this traffic was full of danger i for the public health n Belguim.—The Minister of Agri- culture admitted the justice of M. Cartayvel's represen- tations, and stated that he would shortly take measures to stop the practice complained of. Horses destined to be utilised as tinned meat should be specially branded. Great precautions would in future be taken with regard to the import trade.
