div.head: MEETING ON THE EDUCATION BILL.
div.p: MEETING ON THE EDUCATION BILL.

On Friday evening under the auspices of the above society a well attended meeting of local teachers and others interested in the education question was held for the purpose of discussing the new Education Bill. The meeting was held in the Bethesda Lecture Hall,and was presided over by Mr. J. F. Moulton, president of the local Teachers' Association. There were also pres3nt Mr. R. Waddington, head teacher of the National Schools, Bolton,who attended as a deputation from the National Union of Teachers. Revs. J. Stafford,T. Bramall.J. Simp- son, and W. Moore, Messrs. D. Lewis, A. R. N3rman, J. Snoddy, J. Cookson, Browne, W. Millington, and B. Crosby, secretary. The secretary read letters of apology from different kcal teachers regretting inability to at- tend the meeting and also from Mr. F. Niel, chairman of the School Management Committee of the Widnes School Board, Mr. Joseph Pritchard, Chairman of the Runcorn School Board, Dr. Gastaldi, Mr. Horabin, and the Rev. T. Brackenbury. The Chairman in epening the meeting said the ques- tion was one of the greatest importance, it was second to none, and the bill was worth their very best consid- eration. If the Bill had been brought forward in the true interest of education it would never have met with the strenuous opposition it had from gentlemen who were thoroughly in earnest on the question. If the Bill was passed in its present form it would be a national calamity and the welfare of the country would consider- ably suffer. They would admit that the hopes of the country were bound up with education. If they had a nation uneducated and untaught they would lose their place in the front rank of the nations of the world. They complained about the keen competition which day by day grew keener with the different nations. In his mind the Bill if passed would put back the hands of the clock and would make England less able to c3mpete than at present with foreign nations. The Bill altogether was a retrograde on*.

Mr. Waddington in his addrewdescribed the Bill as a statute of limitations and an attempt to crystallize education at the low ebb at • which it stood to day. The authority that Bill pro- posed to create was not an ideal one, and would not bring about the national system of education which they all desired. It would not repair the omission of 1870 when Mr. Forster threw on one side a golden oppor- tunity of creating a national system of education. The struggle that had since taken place between the two systems voluntary and national had done much to mili- tate against the true interests of natienal edueation.The authority ought to be elected specifically for the purpose of education. (Applause.) He contended that the statutory committee to be formed by the County Coun- cil would consist largely of clergy and fanatics who had beaten the big drum on public platforms. Great harm had been done to the Church of England by the eccen- tricities and fanaticism of many of the clergy. Dealing with the financial aspect of the Bill, Mr. W addington described the effect of the dual system. They had one system at starvation point. They had heara often on public platforms of the sacrifices made by voluntary school managers for the maintenance of the schools but they heard very little of the sacrifices ef the teachers. (Applause.) There was. a difference of 10s. between the voluntary income and that of the local school income and of that 10s., 9s. was accounted for in the difference in the salaries of the teachers. Plainly put it would take lf millions to put the two systems on a level footing anci one million of that would be required to bring the wages of voluntary teachers up to that of the board school teachers. He wanted that million in the interest of the teachers and in the interest of the schools. He objected to the parsi- mony of the managers always being practised in the schools of the workers. If there was one thing more than another upon which the nation ought to be liberal it was in its expenditure on the education of the democracy. Rightly or wrongly they had placed in the hands of the democracy the future of the nation and the best insurs rice the nation could secure was to make the democracy so intel- ligent as to be able to understand the questions they wcre asked to decide. From the political standpoint the money eoent on education gave an adequate return. In 1870, 70,000 people were held in bondage for offences against the common laws, and in 1894 that number was reduced to 35,000 and a number of gaols were also closed. £lO per head was the average spent upon a child in secondary schools but Mr. Balfour maintained that 39s was ample for the child of the worker. IF it was dealt with according to its necessities it woul I have twice as much money spent upon it as the upper class person. He (Mr. Waddington) gave statistics to prove that the Board Schools were not more than adequately staffed while the voluntary schools were very greatly undermanned, and the teachers of the latter had in ad- dition to work in insufficient and insanitary buildings. With regard to the proposed 4s. grant he urged that there ought to be placed in the Bill a clause making it compulsory that the rate of voluntary contributions should be maintained at the level of the average for the past five years. The speaker pointed out the unfair rate of payment given to voluntary school teachers, when compared with the payment given to the Board School teachers. In respect of payment the Catholic teachers were the worst paid in the whole country, and if they belonged to the teachers' union it would be a disgrace to that union to allow them to continue under the condi- tions which they worked in at the present time. At the present time voluntary contributions in a very great many instances only existed on paper. He instanced one school with an average attendance of 955 where £1,300 was obtained from Government grant and, there was placed down for voluntary contributions £634. The salaries of the teachers amounted to £1,200, and £965 was put down asspent upon lighting, cleaning, rent and repairs which meant that 253. per head was spent upon education, and 20. was given to the school cleaner and the rent collector. (Shame.) He urged that the accounts of all schools receiving public ninney should be strictly audited by a Government auditor. Speaking on the religious part of the question bethought if it were left to the parents the greatest difficulty would be solved at once. All the parents cared for was the teachings of the first principles of Christianity witheut the particular dogmas of any sect. That the clergy had not the interest in the teaching of religion in day schools as they proposed, was shown by the fact that as inspector was needed at £l,OOO per year to go to the voluntary schools to see th tt religion was tsueht. In concluding he urged the teachers to forget that they belonged to this section or that section. Their work was not political nor denominational, Their object ought to be to find how that Bill was worked and to criticize it from the standpoint of the man who would have; to carry out the conditions laid down in it. (Applause.) Mr. A. R Norman proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Waddington for the address he had given, and Mr. Srioddy seconded the resolution which was carried.

Mr. A. R. Norman proposed the following resolution : " (1) That this meeting approve; of the creation of Local Authorities for County and County Borough areas to administer both primary and secondary edaca- tion.but is convinced that such authorities should be di- rectly elected ad hoc by the electors in each COA nr v and county borough respectively. (2) That if the Local Authorities be appointed as is proposed in the Bill, they should by statute include invariably :—(a) Members of School Boards; (b) Members of Voluntary School Com- mittees ; (c) Teachers working in schools, and (d) other persons interested in education as such, within the re- spective area;." [le believed from appear- ances that the County Council would become the Education Authority, and that being so it would be well if the authorities shculd include invariably members of school boards, mem- bers of voluntary committees and others SS stated in the resolution. It had been said that school boards had gone too far, but he cduld not see what thnv had done amiss. Since school boards were formed 26 years ago no one would deny that education had made rapid strides to the goal many of them would like to SPA it reach. The improvement in the education of children had been very great indeed, and RS Mr. Waddington had pointed out the crime statistics had been reduced, and they were better preparing their children to fight the battle of competition with other nations, which showed that the money had been well spent. rhey ought not to allow to weigh with them little local considerations, but ought to look upon the matter as *a national ques- tion, and take a broad and national view of the matter. Mr. Waddington seconded, and the resolution was carried.

Mr. T. Bramall proposed.and Mr. Browne seconded the following resolution " lhat in the opinion of this meet- ing (1) The Education Authority, however appointed, should be empowered and rsquired to appoint a repre- sentative or representatives as managers upon each Com- mittee of Voluntary Schools receiving the special aid grant. The Bill should also include (2) Provi<ine for means of appeal by teachers against dismissal from their employment, and (3) Prohibition against grants being given to any school in which teachers are required as a condition of appointment to, or continuance 'n, employ- ment, to undertake or abstain from the !performance of extraneous ani non-scholastic tasks. The resolution was carried. The third resolution was carried on the motion of Mr. D. Lewis seconded by Mr. Snoddy and read as follows— That this meeting (1) protests against proposals to pro- hibit School Boards for raising the sums necessary to ensure the efficiency of Board Schools; and (2) condemns the proposal to limit in all schools the Pa,rliamentary and Fes Grants to the sums now received or to a tnarr- Mum rate of £1 93. In view of the growing popular (10- mands for more complete and effectual primary educa- tion this meeting considers (3) that the income of petit- ols should be adjusted from tio3e to time to the necessities of the situation, and should not be fixed at any maxi- mum rate, though a minimum is justifiable and desir able ; and (4) that the Education Authority should not dispense any grant to schools in which the salaries paid to thettaff are unsuitable and insufficient. Mr. Crosby proposed and Mr. J. Simpson seconded a resolution to the effect that this treating considers (1) the proposed Special Aid Grant inadequate for its pur- po;e ; that (2) the Bill does not aff.rd sufficieot safe- guards that this grant shall be spent on" improving the teaching staff as regards number, qualificatbn, or,

salary " • that (3) no differentiation should be set up between 'Voluntary and Board Schools, as such, in the dispensation of tho Special Aid ; and that (4) the aim of the Bill should he to aid poor Voluntary and Board Schools on the same basis of distribution, rattier than to give the same rate of special aid to all, irrespective of local needs.

The resolution was carried as was a resolution pro- posed by Mr. W. Millington and Rv. J. Stafford as follows : That this meeting deplores the proposed revis- ion of the arrangements for religious instruction laid down in the Elueation Act, 1870, being convinced that the working of tho Co wper-Ternple Clause has fully sat- isfied those most interested in the matter. viz. : the parents of the blildren attending the schools. This meeting foresees in the proposed revision of that clause a vast amount of unnecessary and deplorable controversy. If the proposals in the Bill are to 130 put in force, this meeting must enter an emphatic protest against the selection of the permanent teachers according to their fitness to give the exceptional denominational teaching which is proposed, and considers that this would lead to the imposition 9f theological tests on teachers. . . . .

A vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the meet- ina. Copies of the resolution have been forwarded to the Right Hon. A. J. Bilfour, Sir J. Gorst, Sir W. Harcourt, Mr. Acland, Sir J. F. Brunner and Mr. J. Ciildat, M.P.

div.head: ANOTHER BODY:FOUND IN THE SHIP
div.p: ANOTHER BODY:FOUND IN THE SHIP
CANAL.

On Tuesday evening, before Dr. Blunt, deputy, coroner, an enquiry wag conducted at the "Dg and Dart," Grappenhall,relative CO the finding of a man's body in the Ship Canal on Sunday morning about eight o'clock. Juhn T. Groodliffe, St,ockton Heath Swing Bridge, said that he saw deceased's body on Sunday morning at six o'clock.He had opened the swing bedge and as the vesel was passing someone shouted that there was a body in the canal. He then went and found a body close to the high-level bridge. He could not get to it, so Ei e gave information to the police about it. It was in the centre of the canal, and he could only see the top of the man's head.

P.C. Thomas said at 7.15 on Sunday morning he was informed about the body being floating in the canal. Ho at once went to Latchford locks and Lot a boat. He took assistance and went down the canal, and about eight o'clock found the body and floated it down to the locks. They got it out and brought it to the "Dog and Dart." The body was clothed. There were no marks of violence. The body had apparently been in the water for over a month. They had no clue as to the deceased's identity as there were no papers upon the body. The deceased was about 50 years of age. Witness had had no infor- mation about anyone being missing during the last month.

Mr. Woodcock,one of the jurymen,rsferred to the fact that the body had been towed to the locks before being pulled out. P.C. Thomas explained that it was impossible for the body to be taken from the water where it was found as the banks were perpendicular for about 301 t. _
A verdict of Found drowned was returned.

CRICKET.

On Saturday a good game was expected to result from the meeting for the first time this season of War- rington and Northern (Liverp )01), and fortunately for the enjoyment ot the spectators on th 3 Arpley enclusure the expectations were realised. Northern is well known as a strong teaTn.and last year when Wallington visited them the game was very close, ending in a draw, which was, however, in favour of Warrington. In the second match when Northern came to Warrington they were beaten by a fair majority. Sill it was not thought that the homesters would have an easy thing on for Satur- day, and the result, a victory for Warrington by 10 runs proves that persons of that opinion were correct.

Tha visitors batted first and the initij couple. Fernie and Pick were met by Conner and Thewlis. The latter tried his hand with the bill for the first tim:s this season,but it will probably not be his last for he bowled both steadly and well. Pick had hardly got going be- fore he lifted the ball high in the air and eventually into the hands of Connor who had just bowled it. In Con- nor's first over Hampson seemed at fault for no less than 6 byes were given. However the wicket keeper soon re- covered his form and only allowed one other to pass him. Thompson now joined Fernie but had to imme- niately return for Connor most dexterously caught him out at slip. Henson now came in and met the deliveries of J. J. Crosfild. Two overs only had been sent when the bails dropped, again leaving Fernie in posses- sion. Oaly for a short time, however, for the ball glancing back Connor terminated his career after an exhibition of very deliberate batting. Tuunicliffe only added one, awl G. flolt and W. K. Fernie entered into partnership. At 14 the former's leg got out of plate, while 18 saw W. K. Fernie clean bowled. Meanwhile S. E.Job had been in and made but a weak defence against J. J. Crosfield. Poggie also faced Fernie and contri- buted 16 runs, and A. Williams was not out for 5. This completed the visitofs' score a`., 89 runs.

The two Crosfields opened the home innings awl corn piled 31 together, S. M. Crosfi,ld being first dismissed for IS.l'oggi having made a splendid catch. Job proved too much for J. J. Croslleld 7 runs later. Thewlis was owled for 4, and Connor and Plomer retired with 1 and 3 respectively. These disasters made the i sue of the game very doubtful. But J. Callrm was making a good stand and being joined by W. 11. Podmore, things looked hopeful. The latter put on the runs rapidly, and was very unlucky in being ma out after placing the leather far across the field. Hampson only added 1 more run, and Shan) went to Callon's assist- ance. Together they batted steadily, and Sharp put on 6 before being caught out. Callon next pl ceti the ball into the hands of Tunnicliffe at point, and re- tired to the pavilion after making the top score of the match, 21. The match was won on Callon's dismissal but Scrimshaw and England added another five runs. Altogether, the match was remarkably even. Fielding on each side was brilliant, Connor especially proving; very useful at slip. J.J. Crosfield was the most success- ful of the bowlers.. This victory makes the tourth of the season for Warrington.

The match at Waterloo on Stturday between War- rington and Northern scond teams was a peculiar one. On the Warrington side nobody was able to score any- thing like a respectable figure but Si!cock who kaocked up the fine total of 112 runs. This figure included 22 fours. But for his valtrAble help the liVarrington team would have been ignominiouslybeaten. Smith, with 13, was the only other of the visitors who reached two fizures. On the home side good batting was general. Six of the eleven ran well into two figures. Fraser made 30 and McGinty 25 not out, while Job put on 27. Evi- dently, the bowling was too strong for Warrington and too weak for Northern. All the same, a victory of only 5 runs was placed to the credit of the homesters.

div.head: DRUNKENNESS.
div.p: DRUNKENNESS.

_ Before Mr. Borron at the Earlestown police station on Monday morning, Thomas Taylor, a tramp, was charged with begging and using filthy language in Back Bridge-street, and was fined is. and costs, and in default was sent to gaol for seven days.—Before Mr. J. W. Emmett at the Earlestown police station on Wednesday morning, James Lowe wsis charged with being drunk in Earlestown on Tuesday, and was discharged.

ACCIDENT ON iiAYDOCK LINE. On Saturday afternoon as a London and North- Western railway engine was bringing a train of loaded coal wagons from Messrs. tt vans and Co.'s Collieries at Haydock by way of the firm's private line, it left the rails just atter passing over the crossing in Crow-lane, all the wheels of engine and tender going off the metals. Messrs Rvans's engine was sent down the line and took the train back to Hay dock, and a staff of men set to work to re- rail the engine. but they only succeeded in putting the tender on the rails. The Railway Co.'s break- down gang from Warrington was sent for,and after arriving at the spot they very shortly got the en- gine on the metals. Neither engine nor tender was damaged, but the line was much injured, one rail being broken. No cause was given for the accident, but one rail appeared to have spread.

div.head: STICK FIEE AT NEWTON.
div.p: STICK FIEE AT NEWTON.

On Monday afternoon about three o'clock a stack of wheat near the farm of Mr. Gilbert Marsh at Back-lane, Newton, was discovered to be on fire. The stack which was close to the road was found to be on fire by Thomas Regan,a man in the employ of Mr. Marsh, who was working five or sir yards away,and it commenced blazing at the side furthest from him. There was no one about at the time, and he raised an alarm. Mr. Marsh and several neighbours hurried to the stack, but it was so dry, and a good wind blowing at the time that the flames got a good hold, and nothing could be done to save it,and the stack was destroyed. The damage is estimated at £5O, covered by insurance. No cause can be assigned for the outbreak. GOOD TEMPLAR&

After 33 years creditable sery ice in the " C " troop of Lancashire Yeomanry Has-are, Sergeant Farrier Thomas Ritchie of Newton, has retired upon his laurels. Mr. Ritchie joined the troop as a private,and three years afterwards he was appointed Sergeant Farrier, a position which he has held with honour to himself and the troop. Puring the whole period of his service he has been present at every inspection and annual training at Southport, and has also attended every church parade of the troop. He is permitted on his retirement to retain his rank of Sergeant Farrier and to wear the uniform of the regiment. GOOD TRMPLA.RE (EBENEZER LODGE). _ _

Sixty-one birds which had been sent there in charge of the Convoyer were liber- ted at 11 20, And the following were the prize win- ners :-Ist, £3 10s. and a pair ot young birds, nom. J. Appleton. owner R. Bartley. 2nd ; £2 and a pair of young hirds,norn. G. N. aylor, owner T. Naylor; 3rd, £1 ss. nom. R. W hittaker, owner stifle, ; 4th 153., nom. IT. Ilibbert, owner It. Whitaker; sth, 10s., nom. S. Baker,. owner G. Sturgess ; 6:h, 103., nom. and owner R. Whitaker; 7th, 10s.,norn. and owner F. Hutchins ;Bth, 10s.,num. J. Abbott, owner F. Hutchins; 9th, 7s. 61.,n0m. and owner S. Swann, 10th, 73. 61.,nnm. and owner P. Naylor; 11th, 7s. 61., nom. S. G. Ward, owner R. Bartley,; 12(,h, 7e.4. 61., nom. and owner R. Bartley. The prizes were dis- tributed the same evening at the club house, Pied Bull hotel, and a smoking concert was held, pre- sided over by Mr. S. Swann, and a very pleasant evening was spent. The following :gentlemen con- tributed to the prize fund, viz: Mr. J. Dorman, £1; Mr. R. Stuart, 1034 Mr. R. Whitaker, 10s.; Mr. G. Sturgess, 55.; Mr. W. Smith, 53.

Mr. A. Holmes,coroner for Salford. held an inquest on Tuesday on the body of Abraham Mills, 60, who lived at 84. Trafalgar•st., Broughton. Deceased was a stone- mason, and about three weeks ago he was openin,4 a bottle of stout when he cut his left wrist,severing an ar- tery. He was attended by Dr. Johnson. Blood poison- ing supervened, and on the 13. h inat.he was removed to the SAlford Royal Hospital,where he died early on Satur- day morning. A verdict of death from blood poisoning was returned.

NEWTON DISTRICT COUNCIL.
The monthly meeting of this Council will be held on Monday next at the Town Hall, Earlestown, when the following amongst other matters will be dealt with.

div.head: SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE.
div.p: SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE.

This committee report that a letter dated May 12th, 1896, was read from the managers' correspondent of sit. Mary's and St. John's Roman Catholic Day Schoels, Newton-le-Willows, in answer to the Clerk's letter enclos- ing copy of communication which the committee had received from the Education Department as to the power of School Attendance Committees to insist upon man- agers of public elementary day schools furnishing them with periodical returns of all absences from school, from whatever cause, and requesting to be furnished with such returns,stating that the managers had always been anxious to supply such returns as long as they hoped such particulars were likely to benE fit. the absentees' attendances ; but now declined to make such returns for reasons set forth, and that they would gladly assign their reasons to the Education Department for so doing. Atter a discussion iti was resolved that the whole of the correspondence, inc uding the letter now read, together with the minutes passed on the subject, be sent up to the Education Department, asking for instructions upon the matter. TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION COMMITTEE. A letter was read from the Secretary of the Joint Technical Instruction Committee of the Viaduct Insti- tute stating that an application for a course of Gilchrist lectures had been favourably entertained, and it was resolved that the committee co-operate with the Joint Technical Instruction Committee in starting the lectures as well as a further course of continuation lectures as provided by the Gilchrist Trustees. HIGHWAYS, &C., COMMITTEE. This committee recommend the purchase of a steam road roller from Messrs. Aveling and Porter of Rochester, for the sum of £3OO (less 2-4- discount) such sum to include an awning and the painting of the name of the Council on the engine. The Deputy Sanitary Inspector reports that the scarlet fever is diminishing very nicely and he hopes that in a few weeks they shall be quite clear. His monthly tolls for street hawking were £5 43. 21. ; market tolls £4l 153. 61. Total, £46 193. Bd. Last year for the cor- responding month total tolls were £25 123. 61. This year the May Queen event on the market brought in £26 33. 61. last year it was let by estimate for £25 for the May Queen and the races.

Several nuisances were reported and the committee resolved that notices should be served for abatement. Toe cornEwittee has also passed the following resolu- tions :—That in future gypsies be not allowed to camp on the market ; that all contracts for paving, kerbing, channelling, fligging, etc., of private streets within the district be let as a whole and not in part ; that the plans for new class-rooms at Earlestown district schools, and seven houses, Wargrave New-road, for Mr. G. f. Clarke be approved and passed. The Chairman reported that the Nightsoil Sub-Com- mittee had now got prepared, agreements— (a) between Lord Newton and the Council. (b) the Council and William Gilbert, Farmer, Wigan Road, Newton-le- Willows, and (c) Thomas Williams, of New Hey Farm, Newton-le-Willows, for nightsoil depots on land in their occupation. Mr. Gilbert's agreement being to receive the nightsoil and other refuse from the whole of Viaduct, Town Hall, Crow Lane, and part of Newton Wards; Mr. Williams' agreement being to receive the nightsoil and other refuse from Wargrave Ward, and, by arrange- ment, the remaining part of Newton Ward.—lt was resolved that this Committee recommend that the Com- mon Seal of the Council be affixed to the aforementioned agreements.

GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE. This committee has accepted the following tenders for the period ending May 31st. 1897 :—Of Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., of Haydock Collieries, for the supply of about 3,000 tons of Arley nuts, or Wigan 4 feet coal screened over a 1 inch screen, each at the rate of seven shillings per ton, delivered at either their Earlestown or Crow-lane sidings. duriag the period from July 15t,1896, to May 31.4, 1897, subject to either or both kinds being delivered at the option of the committee ; of too Whitecross Co., Limited, Sherdley Collieries, St. Helens, for the supply of about 1.000 tons of cannel (washed cannel nuts), at the rate of 9.3. 3d. per ton, de- livered at Earlestown railway siding during the period commencing July Ist, 1696, to May 31st, 1897 ; of the Earl of Bradford Colliery Co., Grea', Lever, near Balton, for the supply of about.soo tons of cannel at the rate of 12s. Bd. per ton, delivered at Earlestown railway siding during the period commencing July 15t,1896,t0 May 31st, 1897 ;of Messrs. James Hawarth and C0.,0f Raven-st.,Bt. Helens, for the supply of Buxton lime, as may be re- quired by the 3ommittee at their gas works for one year ending May 31st, 1897, at the rate of 123. per ton delivered at Earlestown Station ; of the United Alkali Company, Exchange Buildings,Liverpool, for the supply of brown vitriol (140 degrees) as may be required by the committee at their gas works, for one year, ending May 31‘t, 1897, filled into the committee's carboys at the Company's Works, St. Helens, at 245. (net) per ton.
GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTER.

__- This committee reports that A letter dated May Bth, 1896, was read from George Haslehurst, Esq„ Local Government Board District Auditor,enclosing newspaper extract. re expenses of members of this Council when away from home on the Council's business ; and stating that" the scale fixed for Poor Law Guardians,etc.,under the regulati-na issued by the Local Government Board under the Conference Act, viz., 7s. 6d. per diem when not away day and night, and 15 per day and night, is the scale in operation in my district (except when in London, when I allow £1 per day and night expenses), which I have to request may be adhered to by your Council." The clerk was in- structed t.) thank Mr. Haslehurst on behalf of the mem- bers of the Council, for his courtesy in pointing out to them what expenses he allows in his district to members when away on the Council's business.

div.head: WHIT-MONDAY AT EARLESTOWN,
div.p: WHIT-MONDAY AT EARLESTOWN,

threatening aspect aysetinodf etlhieghwtfeualtiyhefirnefc,ratnhae twobrDouepgs prheittvei otuhse days,thre contentment to the hearts of hundreds of chil- dren and adults. All the works and places of business in Earlestown, Newton, and Haydock, were closed, and there was consequently a large number of holiday seekers. At Haydock the colliers ceased work on Fri- day evening,aed did not resume until Wednesday morn- ing. There wac no attraction in the village, and a large number of people spent Whit-Monday in other places. The Viaduct works at Earlestown„ closed on Monday; the Vulcan Foundry, on Monday and Tues- day ; Messrs. Slee and Co., the same days, and Messrs. T. and T. Vic as on Monday only. There was a large exodus of p?ople to various places, and the boakings at the station were fairly heavy. The chief and only attraction in the town was the procession of Nonconformist Sunday schools, and with propitious weather, the turn-out was a remarkable fine one. At 10 o'clock all the schools mustered on the Mar- ket ground, and led by the Earlestown brass band sang, under the conductorship of Mr. T. Clam, the hymns, "Arise and sing," and " March, march along." They afterwards filed eff in the following order, Mr. G. F Clarke Acting as chief Marshall :—Earlestown Prins Band, Farlesrown Wesleyan Sunday school, 480: Vulcan Wesleyans, 200 ; Salvation Army and band, 106; Bap- tists, 210 ; Welsh Wesleyans. 91 : Sutton-road Prize Band, Primitive Methodists 315. With the Earlestown. Wesleyans were the Rev. J. H. Bartley; Messrs. T. Clare, W. Clare, George Clarke, J. R. Barr, H. Taylor, .1. H. Profit, and .1. Gooding. The Vulcan Wesleyans on this occasion displayed their beautiful new banner, and leading them were Messrs. Grundy and Martin ; Bap- tists, Rev. F. E. Muller ; Welsh Waalevans, Messrs. Evans J. Williams and M. Watkins: Primitive Metho- dists. Rev. E. R. Davies, Messrs. Banton, Clarke, Ormand and Diekens. The total number in the proces- won was over 1,400. The route taken by the procession , was by Market-it., Queen-st., Houehton-st., Derby-st., Hotel-it.. Cross-lane, Bridge-at., Earl-st., to Earl Cot- tages. returning by way of Bank-st., Wood-st., Viaduct- st., Regent-st., Sankey-st., Market-st., to the Market ground. where after singing the hymn" Lo! I am with you alwaY." and the Doxology, the children dispersed to their various schools. After leaving the ground the Wesleyan school proceeded to the residence of the Rev.J. Batley, where they sang a couple of hymns. Each of the sehools carried their large banners, and the children were well supplied with bannerettes. In the afternoon the annual field day and treats were held, particulars of which will be found below :

div.head: EARLESTOWN WESLEYANS.
div.p: EARLESTOWN WESLEYANS.

At two o'clock the sch Mars assembled on a larae field behind Messrs. T. and T. Vicars' Works,kindly placed at the disposal of the officials by Mr. T. Sanderson. He re they amused themselves until about 4.30,wh0n a proces- sion was formed and they marched to the schoolroom, where they were regaled with a substantial tea. They afterwards returned to the field, and amused themselves in vatious ways up to dusk.

div.head: VULCAN WESLEYANS.
div.p: VULCAN WESLEYANS.
The scholars mustered at the sehrsolrogNm.anii marcile4 to a field lent by Mr. Williams of New Hey Farm. Tea was partaken of in the field,and the afternoon was spent in games of various kinds.

div.head: SALVATION ARMY.
div.p: SALVATION ARMY.

The members of the Army inustered at the Barracks and afterwards marched to Burtotiwood to a field kindly placed at their disposal by Mr. J. Worsley of Derby Farm. Tea was provided in the field, and the alternsan was pleasantly spent.

div.head: BAPTISTS.
div.p: BAPTISTS.

The scholars assembled at the school, and marched in procession by way of Crow-lane, and Mr. T. Molyneun's farmyard to the Earlestown football fipld. T,m, was served on the fi9ld, and a very pleasant afternoon was spent in games of various kinds. WELSH WESLEYANS
Spent the aPernonn in a field ackiining that in which the Brunswick WesleyaLs were assembled. They had tea on the ground, and a pleasant time was passed.
PRIMITIVE itIETFIODISTS.
The scholars assembled at the school and marche.l field lent by Mr. Worsley, near the Railway Arches. Tea NvaS served in the field, and games were indulge in lin- til dusk.

AN IMPUDENT BURGLARY AT WARRINGTOg. 03, Early on Saturday morning a burglary wag c°„'.d mitted a the shop of Mr. Ince, stationer, Winwick-street, Warring Lon, the stances of which show that unusual daring Li% determination were possessed bythe thieves. 1,11 burglar or burglars evidently had a small boy w'ts them for ingress had been effected by removing, small window at the back which it would v" impossible for a grown man to get through. Everhie room in the house had been entered, including sleeping chambers of the occupants, and drove': newsagent a and receptacles ransacked, but so skilfully that .11.11" one was dis?urbed. The thieves carried away 01", them a considerable sum of money. The police ar" investigating the affair.

PIT BATHING-.—A NARROW ESCAPE. Oa Tuesday morning a number of boys _tre,re batlaing in pits in an old brickfield between v",,lr wick-read and Hallam-lane when one of the':': Jarvis Taylor by name, seven years of age,living : Haydock-st., got out of his depth and was in , minent peril of being drowned as the water vilw about thirteen feet deep. A youth named Wi Leather, of 17, Gee-sr., 16 years of age, me beil apprised of the boy's danger, ran to the pit 084 courageously plunged into the water. He succeed,.A in re.;nuing Taylor, who was in a very exhaustn state. but after a short time he somewhat recover's" and proceeded home. FUNERAL OF THE LATE Mns. R. GRER NALL. The White Star liner Teutonic reached Liverpool on Wednesday, and among her passengers .werc Sir Henry Irving and Miss Ellen Terry, who, with their company, have just Concluolecl a tour in the United States. Sir Flenry,in the cour,e of conversation, said that the tour, which had extended over eight or nine months,had been a most rleasant end successful one. The play. of "King Arthur," he continued,had a most flittering reception is the States.and two small new pieces which be brought out, " A Christmas Story," and" Godfried and Uhland," were Very favourably received. The recent difficulty between Great Britain and America regarding Venezue!a having been Inentione:, Sir Henry said he did not come across the slightest evidence of the strained relations oc- casioned thereby—uslese, indeed, it was that the people seemed more enthusiastic towards them than ever.
